subtopic: MR. KNOWLES-ERRORS IN PRINTING OF PROVISIONAL STANDING ORDERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege, notice of which I sent to Your Honour in writing at nine o'clock this morning under the provisions of the new Standing Order 41A. I have also discussed it with Your Honour, with the officers at the table and with the Government House Leader who is unfortunately not able to be here at this moment.
My point relates to two rather major errors in the Provisional Orders which we adopted last week as printed in the appendices to Friday's Hansard and Friday's Votes and Proceedings. The first error relates to the new Standing Order 15A, the one that provides for the allocation of time. The special committee of nine which brought in a report Friday morning recommended amongst other things the inclusion of a new paragraph 9. That paragraph has been omitted from page 2309 of Hansard and from page 6 of the appendix to Votes and Proceedings for Friday. In both cases the new paragraph 9 needs to be inserted and the old paragraph 9 needs to be renumbered as paragraph 10. This error was not made in the body of Votes and Proceedings, but it was made in the appendix to Hansard and the appendix to Votes and Proceedings in both the English and the French editions.
The second error relates to Standing Order 6, section 2. During the discussion of this matter in Committee of the Whole on Thursday this section was amended by inserting therein a new sentence which reads as follows:
During an extended period, as provided under the provisions of this section, no order shall be called for consideration unless such order was under consideration prior to the normal hour of adjournment.
The record of that amendment having been passed will be found in Hansard for Thursday, June 10, at page 2211. However, in Friday's Hansard at page 2307, in Votes and Proceedings at page 3 of the appendix and
also in the body of Votes and Proceedings at page 224, inserting this additional sentence has resulted in a certain amount of garbling so we have several lines that really do not make any sense. This same error appears in the French editions, in the appendices to both Hansard and Votes and Proceedings, but the French edition of the body of Votes and Proceedings does not carry this particular error.
Obviously, Mr. Speaker, I am not attaching any blame for these errors. They are the kind of errors that could easily be made last week. It was obvious also to Your Honour when I discussed this matter with you this morning, and I am sure it will be obvious to all hon. members, that the working documents we will need for the rules of the House should be correct. I suggest, therefore, that the appendices that were added to Hansard and Votes and Proceedings on Friday might be reprinted correctly and made appendices to Hansard and Votes and Proceedings for today.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING MEMBERSHIP AND AGENDA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am leaving later this day to attend the Commonwealth Prime Ministers' Conference which opens in London on June 17. All members of the Commonwealth will be represented at this conference by their Prime Ministers or by Ministers designated by the Prime Minister, I believe, in one or two instances.
The members of the conference will now include-and this is quite a change, as my right hon. friend will recall, from days not so long ago at Commonwealth Prime Min-
isters' meetings-the following in order of seniority inside the Commonwealth: Great Britain, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, India, Pakistan, Ceylon, Ghana, Malaysia, Nigeria, Cyprus, Sierre Leone, Tanzania, Jamaica, Trinidad and Tobago, Uganda, Kenya, Malawi, Malta, Zambia and Gambia; 21 members in all.
All but four of these countries have been admitted to the Commonwealth since 1947. Indeed, all but seven have joined the Commonwealth since 1957. Of the 21 members three are from Europe, if you include the islands of Cyprus and Malta-I am not certain where they belong geographically-three are from the western hemisphere, two from Australasia, four from Asia and nine from Africa.
It is not the custom at these conferences to have an agreed and formal agenda before a conference begins, but the agenda which will be submitted on Thursday by the host Prime Minister, Mr. Wilson of the United Kingdom, I think I can say without impropriety will include the following items which I have no reason to believe will not be formally adopted as items of the agenda:
(a)	The world political situation, and under it the following subheadings: problems in Asia and the Far East, which will include the Indonesian-Malayan difficulty, Viet Nam, and relations generally with China.
(b)	Problems in Africa, and this undoubtedly will include consideration of the question of Rhodesia and the present situation there.
(c)	Problems in Europe.
(d)	East-west relations generally.
(e)	Disarmament and United Nations peace keeping problems.
Then the question of the progress toward independence of British dependant territories which have not yet reached independent status will come up for discussion, and it may well be that the question of Rhodesia will be discussed under this item rather than the one I have just mentioned.
Then there will be a discussion of economic affairs, the general world economic situation, the possibilities of developing inter-Commonwealth trade, and problems of economic development generally. Also, Mr. Speaker, the question of a Commonwealth secretariat, which was considered at the last meeting, will be discussed in terms of the terms of reference of the secretariat and the appointment of a secretary general.
Finally, Mr. Speaker-and this is a matter that was mentioned in the House of Com-
June 14, 1965	COMMONS
mons the other day-there will be discussed the question of a Commonwealth parliamentary assembly, which was suggested by the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom.
That is all I think I can usefully say about the meeting at this stage. When I return I will, of course, be happy to report to the House about the conference. I think I can say with some assurance that the meeting, which will be considering matters of very great importance to the Commonwealth and to the world in which the members of the Commonwealth play such an important part, will further strengthen the relationships among the members of this great association of free nations which now spans all the continents.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING MEMBERSHIP AND AGENDA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the privilege that comes to a Prime Minister to attend a Commonwealth Prime Ministers' Conference is one of the most challenging opportunities that can come to anyone.
The Prime Minister has spoken of the tremendous growth of the Commonwealth, pointing out that of the present membership of 21 all but seven have joined since 1957. The expansion has been phenomenal, and the past informality of these conferences has been maintained despite this increase in the membership.
My first words to the Prime Minister will be words of good wishes in the mission that he goes on. I wish him Godspeed and a return with that inspiration which comes from attendance at such conferences.
He has mentioned some of the matters that will arise. One of them has to do with further transitions from colonialism to independence, and I have but one word to add in that connection. In 1961 and 1962 I took the stand in the Prime Ministers' Conference that no nation within the Commonwealth should permit itself the luxury of practising discrimination as a foundation or principle. That today is accepted, but I should like to add that in my opinion no nation, no colony desiring to join this commonwealth, should be accepted if its political philosophy constitutes support for communism. I think this is a necessary consequence and should be accepted as a principle of membership. To do otherwise would be to place the members of the Commonwealth in the position of having within their ranks those who would destroy that parliament of nations bound together
DEBATES	2315
Commonwealth Conference neither by seal nor sword but constituting for the world an example of what freedom loving nations can achieve when operating in concert.
Mention was made of one or two matters which will come up for consideration. One is the idea of a commonwealth secretariat. As an experiment in bringing about closer unity I think a secretariat could perform a worthwhile function in providing a continuing group for the exchange of information and an understanding of the problems of other members. But I do hope we shall not give adherence to a secretariat having executive powers. The other day I asked a question regarding the Commonwealth Assembly. I had hoped we might have found some time to discuss this question. We all recall the days of Joseph Chamberlain, who envisaged a new concept of empire in which representatives of the component parts would meet at Westminster. With the passing years that concept has been outgrown and outmoded. Call it what you will, I hope the Prime Ministers will not come to a conclusion that anything in the nature of a representative or parliamentary institution should be set up within the Commonwealth.
My reasons for that are simple. First, such a step would be a retrograde one; and second, if determinations of policies were to be made or recommended, then you would have a central institution which would vote, which is the only way in which democratic assembly decisions can be made. If there is one thing that we must guard against in the Commonwealth-and this applies particularly to the Prime Ministers' Conference-it is that. We should never have a vote. If we were to establish within the Commonwealth, at the Prime Ministers' Conference, the exercise of a vote by the various component, representative countries, it would not be very long before the Commonwealth would cease to exist; for none of us, I think I can say-certainly not Canada, and I know of no other country-would accept the principle that a majority vote among Commonwealth Prime Ministers would in any way be acceptable.
Then there is a third matter, and the Prime Minister did not refer to this. It has been suggested that there should be a Commonwealth court to adjudicate on disputes that arise between member nations within the Commonwealth. Personally I think such an institution might toe an effective one. I realize that there are arguments against it; but at the same time when I think of the situation now existing between India and
June 14, 1965

Commonwealth Conference Pakistan in reference to the Rann of Hutch area and other disputes that I could speak of, I ask myself whether there is any reason that the nations of the Commonwealth should not be able to make one further advance and bring about the establishment of a court, a constitutional court if you will, to deal with matters arising between Commonwealth countries.
I am not going to say anything about the unfortunate events of the last two or three days in Ottawa in connection with this matter, but I do feel that so long as there are disputes between the member nations of the Commonwealth and no means of solving them except through the instrumentality of the Prime Ministers' Conference and other diplomatic, behind the scenes discussion, the acceptance of the principle of a Commonwealth constitutional court is not beyond possibility. It might indeed provide for the settlement of matters that at the present time seem almost insoluble.
I would repeat to the Prime Minister what I said earlier. We wish him well. We hope the conference will be a success. These conferences pass from year to year creating new precedents. My own impression is that we are closer in the Commonwealth today than we were 15 years ago, and the reason for that relationship is the fact that each of the nations endeavours to understand the other and under the Queen, either as Sovereign or as head of the Commonwealth, we bring before the world an example of what nations dissimilar in colour and religion, from all parts of the world and in all states of economic development, can achieve when there is a will to do so.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING MEMBERSHIP AND AGENDA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure we all desire to thank the Prime Minister for giving us some idea of the various items which will be discussed at the Commonwealth Prime Ministers Conference, and I am sure the people of Canada hope the results of these consultations and deliberations will be beneficial not only to Canada but to the world at large.
In these days of power blocs there is a good deal of cynicism about the role which a free association of free nations can play in world affairs. My own personal view is that the Commonwealth has an important role to play. While it does not have a central government and is not bound together by binding treaties, it does bring together Governments of peoples from every part of the world including Asia, Africa, Europe, the
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l
western hemisphere and Australasia, and enables peoples of many tongues and races to meet together with a common loyalty to common democratic objectives.
I think such a meeting cannot do anything but good. Only time, of course, will prove whether or not this free association of free people can play an important part in world affairs. I feel certain that in view of the type of men who will be representing the Commonwealth at this conference they will be capable of making a great contribution.
I am glad to see that the matter of Commonwealth trade is going to be discussed. Commonwealth trade is unfortunately very much like what Mark Twain said about the weather; everybody talks about it, but not very much is done about it. There are great possibilities within this field, and Canada with its present imbalance of payments could benefit from expanded Commonwealth trade. I trust out of these discussions some policies and trade negotiations will be set up which will increase Canada's trade with other parts of the Commonwealth.
I hope the same opportunity will be given for discussions in respect of external aid within the Commonwealth. As the Prime Minister knows, I have frequently suggested that one of the things Canada might well consider is concentrating its external aid efforts on Commonwealth countries within the western hemisphere, adopting them as our special consideration. I am not suggesting that we should do less elsewhere but that we should do more for those small nations that have very serious economic problems and that are at our back door. In this category there are both French and English areas in the western hemisphere. These are areas which we could help very easily, and with which we have close contact. This is one area of assistance that might be discussed at this Conference.
I am sure all Members of this House, certainly the Members of this group, wish the Prime Minister well as he goes to the Conference. We trust and are sure that Canada will be ably represented, and we are proud to have the Prime Minister speak on behalf of the people of Canada. We wish him well and hope he will have a very happy and successful trip.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING MEMBERSHIP AND AGENDA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege to join with others in this House in thanking the Prime Minister for outlining the program he expects to be dealing with at the coming Commonwealth Conference, and also in wishing him success
June 14, 1965	COMMONS
in the particular role, of which I am very-conscious, that he will be carrying on at this particular Conference. We know of the number of delicate problems which will be dealt with and the rather unique position he presently holds in the confidence of the Prime Ministers of the Commonwealth. We know also the responsibility he faces and that this Conference will not be an easy one.
It is rather significant that this Conference is to be held just preceding the Afro-Asian Conference. Last year the Commonwealth Prime Ministers' Conference was held just before the African Unity Conference at Cairo, and we know how much influence the Commonwealth Conference had on some of those who played an important role in the OAU Conference. It might likewise be anticipated that this Conference will have a good influence on the outcome of the Afro-Asian Conference which follows it.
It is also rather unique that this year-and I think this places special focus on the importance of this years' Conference-is the 750th anniversary of the Magna Carta and the 700th anniversary of the first parliamentary government. Certainly there is a tremendous lesson in this fact particularly for the newer members of the Commonwealth. There is no doubt that the greatest heritage we have from Great Britain is that tradition of parliamentary Government such as we follow here in our parliamentary set-up. This is something very necessary today in the world if the freedoms of the individual and the potential development of free democratic processes are to be fulfilled in these newer countries as well.
I found the remarks of the Leader of the Official Opposition interesting when he referred to the fact that, if things continue as they are now, it might well be possible that the Commonwealth will include a nation with a communist-in dined government. I join with him in questioning whether such could be possible in view of the tradition of parliamentary democracy that is so characteristic of the Commonwealth. It is important, however, to remember that in respect of these problems he voiced there are similar conditions at present which might be just as difficult to reconcile with a parliamentary Government and which threaten to remove from some of the associated Commonwealth nations some of the genuine freedoms of a democratic way of life.
We noted that the Prime Minister mentioned a number of the important items on the agenda. We are particularly conscious
DEBATES	2317
Commonwealth Conference of the decision that is to be made as to whether there is to be a Commonwealth secretariat. It was of interest to note this morning that the Australian Prime Minister has already voiced his opposition to such a set-up. On the other hand, we in Canada have one of the leading contenders for the position of Secretary General of such an organization. Certainly the future of the new Commonwealth is closely related to this decision, and to the decision as to whether there might be a Commonwealth parliamentary assembly.
These decisions, I am sure we all agree, are those which will determine the direction the Commonwealth will take in future years. I am sure that out of this current meeting decisions will be forthcoming which will set the course for the new Commonwealth which I am confident is going to emerge, and which must come about if in the years ahead it is to carry out its responsibility with the same degree of success it has had in past years.
Therefore we join with all Members of this House in wishing the Prime Minister and those who will accompany him great success at this very important and responsible meeting of the Commonwealth.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER RESPECTING MEMBERSHIP AND AGENDA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) will soon leave to attend the conference of the Commonwealth prime ministers. I hope he arrives in London in time to attend the decoration ceremony of the "Beatles" who were made members of the Order of the British Empire. In my opinion, this will be a memorable ceremony, and the Prime Minister of Canada should attend it.
Some 40 years ago, more precisely at the end of the first World War, my father was created commander of the Order of the British Empire. But times have changed since; we do not hear any more about the British Empire, except as regards decorations. We hear about the Commonwealth; the institution formerly called the British Empire has become a democratic association of free countries which discuss on an equal footing their common problems.
I express the wish that the discussions which will take place at the forthcoming commonwealth Prime Ministers' conference will benefit all member countries.
The Prime Minister referred to the possible setting up of a commonwealth parliamentary assembly. I wonder what would be the purpose of establishing such an assembly, when

June 14, 1965
Questions
we already have the commonwealth parliamentary association, an informal association without any official jurisdiction.
What problems would this commonwealth parliamentary assembly discuss? Would it have to make certain decisions on behalf of commonwealth countries? Which matters would come under its jurisdiction?
Mr. Speaker, I wonder if that type of Commonwealth Assembly is indicated, or if it would not rather tend to withdraw certain privileges from each of its members.
I do wish the Prime Minister an excellent trip to England. I am sure the members of the house will, in the meantime, endeavour to accomplish as much as possible in the way of adopting legislation so that, upon his return, he can give us a report on his trip and the discussions that will have taken place. I also hope the legislative program he proposed last week will have been completed, for the welfare of the Canadian people, and that he will be pleased with the work performed during his absence from the house.
We, therefore, wish him "bon voyage" and, in the meantime, we will attend to adopting as many legislative measures as possible.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL, JOINT COMMISSION-GREAT LAKES WATER LEVELS
speechtext:

I have been informed by the Canadian section of the International Joint Commission that the public hearings referred to were the preliminary sessions conducted by the Commission to give the customary opportunity to those interested to submit information and views on the problem under reference. They were held in Toronto; Sault Ste. Marie, Michigan; Windsor; and Chicago. The testimony given at these sessions by the 47 witnesses who appeared and the briefs submitted are presently under study by the Commission and its advisers.
2. I have been informed by the Canadian section of the International Joint Commission that the information and proposals submitted related primarily to the need of regu-22620-1481
lation of lake levels and the effects of specific levels on the various interests involved. The statements were for the most part non-technical in nature.

The terms of the Great Lakes Levels Reference transmitted to the International Joint Commission by the Governments of the United States and Canada quite properly confined its investigation and study to the natural drainage of the Great Lakes which constitute international or boundary waters. The Grand Canal scheme proposed by Mr. T. W. Kierans of Sudbury involves the utilization of resources owned by the Provinces of Ontario and Quebec. It is proposed that investigation and study of this scheme and other possibilities for diversion of Ontario and Quebec waters into the Great Lakes drainage be undertaken nationally under arrangements worked out between the federal and Ontario and Quebec provincial authorities.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise tor the purpose of making a motion on a matter of public importance which in my opinion is of sufficient urgency to require immediate debate. As you know, there is a medical services insurance bill before the Ontario legislature, which is now in the committee stage. If this bill passes it will provide voluntary coverage subsidized after a means test, and with minimal benefits, all of which features are in strong contrast to the Hall Commission recommendations.
If this bill passes in its present form it will be extremely difficult, if not impossible, to implement a national medical services plan. As Ontario is Canada's largest province and has the highest per capita income, a national scheme could not possibly function without its participation. In this connection I wish to quote very briefly from the Hall Commission report.

It becomes evident that a formula must be sought on a national scale, with Federal-Provincial agreement on programs to ensure the provision and distribution of resources for the achievement of the best possible health care...for all Canadians.

is correct. However, the motion which the hon. Member for Hamilton South has moved does not deal with medicare by itself; it deals with medicare in relation to the fact that a plan is now being dealt with in the Ontario Legislature which, if passed, would jeopardize the establishment of a comprehensive health insurance program for Canada. Therefore the subject matter of the motion moved by the hon. Member is quite different from a general discussion of medicare such as we had in the Speech from the Throne debate.
The second objection taken by the Minister of Labour is that this deals with something outside the jurisdiction of this House. I suggest the motion does nothing of the kind. The motion deals with the failure of the Government to act on something which is directly within the purview of this House, namely the steps which are necessary to implement the recommendations of the Hall Commission. The hon. Member's reference to what is happening in the Ontario House is merely used as illustrative of the fact that the Province of Ontario, in addition to several other Provinces, is taking legislative action which if carried to its ultimate conclusion will make it very difficult to establish a national health insurance program in Canada.
May I say just a word while I am on my feet on the matter of urgency. It is now a year since the Hall Commission brought down its report. One of the recommendations of the Commission was that within six months of the report being received by the Government of Canada, a Federal-Provincial conference should be called to lay the necessary plans for the implementation of this report. This has not been done, and because it has not been done several Provinces, British Columbia, Alberta and now Ontario, are proceeding with provincial plans which in the main are to be based on administration by private professional groups and insurance companies.

speechtext:
Your Honour must be grateful for all the assistance you get from the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice.
Because of the action which several Provincial Legislatures are taking it has become imperative that the Parliament of Canada should act, and act promptly, if the Hall Commission recommendations are ever to be implemented. For that reason it is urgent that this matter be discussed, and be discussed without any further delay. The fact that in the Ontario Legislature the opposition parties, both the Liberal Party and the New Democratic Party, are asking for a health insurance plan which would be Government sponsored and Government operated, as suggested by the Hall Commission, lends support to the idea that the matter of who will administer this plan should be settled now.
Our argument on urgency is that if the Government of Canada favours a Government sponsored and Government operated plan as recommended by the Hall Commission, it should say so now before provincial Governments take action which will make it virtually impossible later on to put the Hall Commission recommendations into effect.
For that reason we think this matter should be debated, and should be debated today. We feel that any further delay will work great hardship on the people of Canada and will prevent a comprehensive health insurance program being established in this country in the foreseeable future.

maintopic: NATIONAL MEDICAL SERVICE-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I suggest that the attempt to move the adjournment of the House under Standing Order 26 by the hon. Member for Hamilton South is out of order for several reasons. The first and most important one, in my view, is that it fails to involve a matter that is within the administrative responsibility of the Federal Government. Citation 100 of Beauchesne's fourth edition states very clearly that the definite matter of urgent public importance for the discussion of which a Member may ask leave to move the adjournment of the House under Standing Order 26 must involve the administrative responsibility of the Government. Quite clearly, at the present time the administrative responsibility for a medicare plan rests within the jurisdiction of the Provinces.
National Medical Service This situation could not change unless there were agreement by the Provincial Governments to transfer that responsibility to the Federal Government.
Now, Mr. Speaker, regardless of the recommendations in the Hall Commission report, these recommendations from a Royal Commission do not transfer the responsibility for this kind of service. I suggest, therefore, that the motion fails in that respect.
The second thing and this was a point that was raised by the hon. Member for Burnaby-Coquitlam-the urgency of debate is to determine who is going to administer a medicare program for Canadians. I suggest at the moment that until there is an agreement between the Provincial Governments and the Federal Government, there is no question but that the jurisdiction lays with the Provincial Governments. This is the reason Alberta, British Columbia, Saskatchewan and now Ontario have gone ahead with these plans within the confines of their area of jurisdiction.
Citation 100 subsection 3, to which I have referred says that urgency does not apply to the matter itself, but it means urgency of debate. It goes on to say that the public interest must demand that the discussion take place immediately. Well, Mr. Speaker, we would then have to decide what substantial progress could be made as the result of having a debate today. I suggest there is absolutely no possibility of transferring jurisdiction over this matter from Provincial Governments to the Federal Government by having a debate today. The motion fails therefore, under the test of urgency of debate and should be ruled out of order.

Mr. Speaker, last week in response-
June 14, 1965

to a question from the hon. Member tor Qu'Appelle I undertook to obtain further details in respect of certain mainland Chinese products, the values for duty of which were the subject of recent directives pursuant to section 38 of the Customs Act.
My Department has not received any so-called "affidavits" alleging that the Chinese products involved are not comparable to the Japanese products on which the appraised values for duty were based. One interested party, however, has made oral representations with respect to one product, namely worsted fabrics, contending that in our comparison of the Chinese goods with similar Japanese goods additional allowances should have been made for quality. Although, as I stated on June 2, in making our appraisals we were cognizant of variations in quality, consideration is now being given to the representations which have been made.
It is not unusual for importers to protest departmental rulings in cases such as this, where values for duty have been increased. We are always willing, however, to consider such representations, and I might add that there are ample provisions in the Customs Act itself for the hearing of appeals and redress of grievances.
The hon. Member also wished me to consider valuing goods from mainland China on the basis of Hong Kong goods. On June 2 I mentioned that the procedure we are now using is in accordance with clause II of Memorandum I of the long term wheat agreement, which was signed by the Canadian Wheat Board and a Chinese import and export corporation in August of 1963.
Clause II provides that goods of a class or kind made in Canada shall "be valued for duty purposes on the same basis as similar Japanese goods or their equivalent, with due regard for differences in quality, finish, construction, et cetera." An exchange of interpretive notes between the signatories modified the provisions of this clause to the extent that Chinese goods could be valued on the basis of Hong Kong goods "in situations where Japanese values cannot be established." It will be obvious that Hong Kong values are to be used only as a second resort.
In view of these provisions and the availability of Japanese valuation data, the directives I issued were in terms of Japanese values. Indeed, it is usually more difficult to establish fair market values in Hong Kong than in Japan, due to the nature of the Hong Kong market, where relatively few sales are made for home consumption.

speechtext: The House resumed, from Tuesday, May 18, consideration of the motion of Mr. Gordon for the second reading of Bill No. C-102, respecting banks and banking.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the end of the discussion on this bill I said that the Commission should suggest that the field of mortgages be reopened to the banks, as was done in 1958. When the rates of interest were increased, some banks withdrew from those fields.
It is also strongly recommended that loans of that nature be granted, more particularly as regards already built houses, in order to alleviate the burden of small owners.

Of course the hon. Member was talking through his hat, and I am not making a pun. He was completely off base, as quite often happens in matters of this kind. After all, we know that the Porter report was only tabled and made available to the public in April, 1964, barely a year ago. Since there had been no such report for 30 years, and since the problem was so complex, the Government required time to examine it and assess public reaction as well as the reaction of the financial world. I believe it was completely wrong to say, as the
[Mr. Pilon.l
hon. Member said so extravagantly, that the House had been delaying this matter for two years. I just wanted to clear up that misconception which may have arisen as a result of that remark.
Now, Mr. Speaker, at the resolution stage a number of speeches were made on behalf of all the parties in this House. I should like to say now that having had an opportunity of looking at the Bill, I think we can agree- certainly I can agree-with an editorial which appeared in the Financial Post in the following terms:
For the first time in 30 years able men Inside and outside government have done the detailed homework to gear our financial machinery to the future. Let us not throw away our chance.
Frankly I think, under these circumstances, as a result of the Royal Commission report, the Government has thrown away the chance. I believe that in many ways this Bill represents a timid approach to the problem. This approach is indicated by the Minister's remarks at the resolution stage. I should like to make some reference to his remarks at that time, when he said that the central theme of the report of the Royal Commission was that financial institutions, particularly banks, should have broader investment and borrowing powers and so become a more competitive and flexible system. He said that the Government was taking a long run view of this matter. The question immediately comes to mind, how long is a long run view? There are certain problems which are not going to go away merely by postponing consideration of them.
I believe one of the problems which the Government has deliberately kept away from is the control of the near banks. This was the central feature of the Royal Commission report, yet there is absolutely nothing in this Bill to cover that subject. I know that at the second reading stage the Minister said the banks represent a much larger segment of the financial community, and since they are under the central banking system the Bank of Canada has certain controls over the chartered banks, the Superintendent of Banking has certain controls over the chartered banks, and whatever control is imposed upon the chartered banks will sort of filter down to the near banks.
I hope the Minister is not serious when he says that, because I am sure he will recognize that there are a number of trust companies not under Federal jurisdiction, for instance. I say immediately that I am not
June 14. 1965

Bank Act
concerned primarily with the operations of those under Federal jurisdiction.
I am concerned about those that are under exclusive Provincial jurisdiction. On May 18 the Minister, rather blithely I thought, indicated that they were relying on the provincial inspection system for these companies, and if it was not up to scratch the effect would not be too great. I am afraid I cannot agree with him. I hope I am not doing him an injustice in paraphrasing his words. I am repeating the strictures I made at the resolution stage. There are some trust and loan companies operating under provincial charter and some of these Provinces have reasonably adequate inspection systems, while in other Provinces I am afraid they do not exist so effectively.
If I may, I should like to repeat what I said at page 1000 of Hansard for May 6, the second column:
In my view, there are a lot of institutions that are carrying on the business of near banking that must be brought under some form of control. Frankly, their operations are very close to the line. It will only take the failure on the part of one or more of these institutions to honour their depositors' credits to start a terrible run, and a lot of people will get hurt. A number of these institutions operate on what I think is a far too narrow principle, in so far as liquid reserves are concerned. They are well over-extended in real estate and construction promotion. It would take but one or two bad breaks for the whole house of cards to tumble.
I hold the same views today. The Government evidently feels that the operations of these institutions may not have too great an effect on monetary policy or in the whole picture of the control of the volume of money. This is a debatable point, and I think it is one which might well be examined in committee. We should like to know, for instance, why the Governor of the Bank of Canada made a certain statement in this regard. It will be very interesting to see why it is thought that the operations of such institutions had such an impact on the monetary supply.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
One has only to consider the remarks of the Chairman of the U.S. Federal Reserve Board the other day, a man who was speaking on behalf of the bankers. We know very well that politically there may be pressures upon him because he went counter to what is an easy credit policy in the United States, but certainly he spoke on behalf of the financial community when he said there are signs, and there can be signs, that some operations may be very dangerous. We have only to reach a flattening out, or to arrive at a plateau in certain types of developments in this country, for a lot of speculative promotions to get into trouble, including some which are being financed by the sort of organizations about which I am speaking.
The Minister indicated that the amendments to the Bank Act were going to deal only with banks. He said he did not feel the Bank Act should deal with the operations of some people who might be brought in under the umbrella if control were extended; he did not think that was a purpose of the Bank Act. I certainly do not think that trust companies which carry on trust business or other activities can escape the supervision of their quasi-banking operations. That is not logical reasoning. If it is intended that banking operations in this country be under supervision, then they too should be under that supervision.
Though the Minister gave his reasons, as recorded at page 1429 of Hansard on May 18, I do not think we have gone into this matter sufficiently, and we will welcome the opportunity of examining him in the Banking and Commerce Committee. Dealing seriatim with the amendments, the Minister said that the operations of the banks would be extended, and he paid tribute to their competitive position.
One does not need to go into the whole history of the banking system in Canada to realize that the banks, by and large, have done a tremendously good job. They provide a very extensive service. I believe there is a branch of a chartered bank in Canada for about every 3,500 people, whereas in the United States the ratio of banks or branches of banks is one for every 5,500 people. From personal experience I know the operations of many bank branches in Canada are not profitable; in other words the branches are not self sustaining. As a matter of fact a lot of the so-called plaza branches in shopping plazas are rendering a public service only. They do collect sums of money, but later I will be discussing the changed nature of the banking system during the past 10 years to show that the number of branches has little relationship to the profit picture. The operation of the banking system as a whole is not successful only because each branch makes a profit.
The Minister indicated that in 1960 and 1961 the banks went into the personal loan field or term plan field and, as a result, interest rates in that field dropped. That is a matter of record. I believe it is generally agreed that in the auto financing field the

hon. gentleman can expect careful examination with regard to it.
I agree with the Minister's remarks about shared ownership and interlocking directorships. I think it is only good sense that there should not be a conflict of interest or domination of the banking system by a small, powerful group.
This limitation of shareholdings to 10 per cent in the case of resident shareholders will not apply to new banks which are being organized. But the bill does not spell out, nor have we been told clearly, how long a bank is to be considered as a "new bank". When will a bank have to regularize, so to speak, its share ownership at 10 per cent? Implicit in the Minister's remarks was a threat to control foreign currency transactions by Canadian banks. The reasons for this are not apparent from anything the Minister may have said. There is also to be a prohibition applied to the establishment by foreign banks of agencies in Canada. This has nothing to do with deposit business; we know an agency cannot accept deposits. This prevents the establishment of any agency in Canada. I do not know how others will view this provision, but the Canadian chartered banks certainly operate agencies. I think immediately of agencies in New York, Chicago and Houston. A number of our banks operate on the basis of agencies-and operate most successfully, I may say. Yet we are about to deny any foreign bank the opportunity to operate in Canada on the basis of an agency. Why is there not to be reciprocity in this regard? Is it because by operating on the basis of an agency a foreign bank would get into Canadian business?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext: Just as I said.

subtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext:
To what extent? Certainly there are ways of getting around this. I do not know what purpose this provision will accomplish unless it is to invite retaliation. I hate to think the Royal Bank might have to close its agencies in New York, Chicago and Houston. Certainly in the oil business there is a tremendous contact through these agencies. I believe that we in Canada, especially as far as the Province of Alberta and the oil industry are concerned, would suffer very much if such a situation ever arose. If this policy is likely to invite retaliation we want to hear the Minister tell us more about it; in particular, why he thinks there may not be retaliation.
One of the last features of the legislation on which I wish to speak has to do with
Bank Act
new banking corporations. This, frankly, is a weird and wonderful thing which has been put before us. The Minister has said that the incorporation of banks should not be the subject of scrutiny, basing himself on abuses of procedure which he says have taken place in the past year or so. We are now to have a change. I believe this will merely be a change from the frying pan into the fire. Under clause 8 letters patent for a chartered bank may be issued by the Governor in Council. If this proposal does not possess all the trappings of patronage I do not know what does. It is certainly susceptible to patronage. I can easily imagine three or four groups applying at the same time for a charter for a new bank. We shall see what happens, particularly when the number of charters to be granted in the wisdom of the Government are less than the number of applications.
At the present time Parliament decides, and the Government exerts its influence with regard to the number of charters which come forward. I doubt whether Parliament or the Government should indulge in any paternalism, but I have placed on record-during the debate on the incorporation of the Laurentide Bank last session, I believe-the number of banks to which charters had been granted but which had never gone into business.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
In any event, here we have a situation where the Government proposes that the Governor in Council shall issue letters patent and that these letters patent shall become effective on the fortieth sitting day of a session after having been laid before the House, unless the letters patent shall have been annulled. It is also provided that within 15 days after the issuance of the letters patent they shall be tabled in the House; and within 15 days thereafter a motion must be made according to form in the House of Commons, signed by at least ten Members, if the letters patent are to be annulled. A debate must then be initiated within four sitting days of the motion being made. But it does not say when the debate must terminate, and strangely enough it says that unless the letters patent shall have been annulled, they shall be in force.
In other words there is a built-in inducement for a Government filibuster. The motion would likely be from the Opposition. If the letters patent are issued by the Cabinet, certainly no ten Government Members are

June 14, 1965
Bank Act
going to stand in their places and put forward a motion to annul those letters patent. Therefore the motion would be from the Opposition side, and the way the Act is worded no decision on an Opposition motion is the equivalent of a negative vote on the motion and the letters patent shall not have been annulled and therefore shall become effective.
I am saying this is theoretical, Mr. Speaker. It may be that now under the rules an allocation of time order should be made, and all that; but there it is in the Act in section 8(5). This is all possible. Therefore I say this is an odd way of revamping the incorporation of chartered banks.
Of course the other place has nothing to do with it. The letters patent are issued from the Governor in Council; the House of Commons alone will have the power of annulment. There is nothing about the Parliament of Canada. In other words Parliament is being bypassed with regard to the control of banking. This Act, however, is going to be an Act of Parliament. This Act will ask the other place to forever set aside their rights respecting the control of banking and the examination of banking in so far as the incorporation of new banks is concerned.
I think we are going to require an explanation in this regard. Why was this formula chosen? Was it because of the temporary embarrassment over the formation of new banks? A few moments ago the Minister answered the Leader of the Opposition in regard to the possibility of Provincial Governments or their emanations investing in either non-voting stock or having bank stock for investment purposes in so far as university trust funds, etc., are concerned. With that part of it I would agree, and I hope we will see something instructive from the committee to this end. The Minister has been quite fair about this. But if that were the case, is it a certainty that there would be this continuing, shall we say partisan objection to the present bank charters because a certain Provincial Premier is not getting precisely what he wants and there is a certain pressure group here acting on his behalf? I do not think this should be so. I think Parliament still has the right to examine chartered banks, and what is being exchanged is going to work something like the old Biblical story of the man who had devils in his house. He left his house; it was swept clean. He returned to live with devils who were seven times more difficult. Frankly, Mr. Speaker, I think this is what is going to

happen, namely that the formula now proposed is going to be even worse than the present one, because there is no safeguard except the allocation of time within the new rules, and there is no guarantee that they will continue beyond the next ensuing session; but we are writing it into the Bank Act, putting it away for ten years.
I consider it a most dubious formula, and I would much prefer to be able to carry on under the present circumstances; because I can assure the Minister that if the same philosophy prevails and this Act goes through, say at the end of this year, and the applications for incorporation come in, the same ten people can stand up, put in their motion for annulment and start the battle all over again; and without any conclusion, either. Therefore I put it to the Minister that this provision in the Act will certainly stand a lot of re-examination.
Mr. Speaker, there are many other things which I could say about the Act that I think I would like to save for the committee hearings or later. I am glad to see that the Minister has recognized the facts of life. This is quite understandable; it could have been predicted months ago that there would have to be an Act extending the provisions of the Bank Act. The Minister has asked for this extension until December 31, 1965. Even that, I think, may be shaving it a little closely; and this is something the Government has to consider. It is all very well to say that this Act shall go to the Banking and Commerce Committee, but if the Minister looks at the calendar he will realize that if there is a summer recess and Parliament does not come back until after September 17, there is going to be precious little time for this voluminous Act to be considered in committee unless there is a special effort made with regard to the committee.
This, of course, is presupposing that the Minister is not going to insist that the committee sit during the summer recess. I realize that the Banking and Commerce Committee is not yet organized. It might be organized by next week, and everyone who wishes to appear will have to be given an invitation. We know what it is like during the summer months, and if the committee does not sit then it will be sitting in October and November, subject to the difficulties of debate in December. Perhaps the session would finish by the end of November, which I suppose is a fond hope.
In view of this, Mr. Speaker, I am just wondering whether the Minister might not
June 14, 1965

be wiser in having the extension to July 1 of next year. This is not to invite extended discussion, but I am looking at the practicalities of the calendar and the consequent limitations on discussion both in committee and in this House.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)

Mr. Speaker, in participating during the second reading stage of this bill, let me say that it is not our intention to delay its passage at all, but that we are hopeful it will receive second reading today and be sent to the new committee, the name of which escapes me at the moment.
One of the things I want to suggest to the Minister for consideration deals with the manner in which the committee will handle this bill in its initial stages. I think an examination of the potential Members of the committee will indicate that there is only one Member who was here during the last revisions of the Bank Act in 1954, and that is my colleague the hon. Member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron). With that exception, most if not all of the Members will be completely unfamiliar with this particular piece of legislation. Of course the bill has some 111 pages and many clauses, and I would urge the Minister to use the first week or two of the sittings of the committee as a real educational program for the Members of that committee. I am sure they would like to have the various officials of the department called to give them a complete background picture of the whole banking and monetary system in Canada. During later consideration, a great deal more headway could be made if at the preliminary meetings a reasonable number of witnesses could be called to lay before the committee a complete picture of the banking and monetary structure in Canada. It would be useful if this could be done before the committee got into detailed discussions of the Act itself.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether my hon. friend would permit a question. Does he not think that perhaps the suggestion he has now made would be more appropriately made to the steering committee of the Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs when it is set up a little later this week?

No doubt this suggestion will be made to that steering committee but, knowing the influence of the Minister and his genial disposition, we thought there would be no harm in putting the bug in his ear, particularly in view of his general disposition to
Bank Act
acquiesce in helpful suggestions made by Members of the Opposition.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext: And because of his powers of persuasion.

subtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext:
Yes, and because of his powers of persuasion over his colleagues. In general, we hope a very clear picture will be given to the Members before they get into a detailed discussion.
We do not at this stage want to say too much about the various clauses of the bill, because they are voluminous and complicated but there are one or two matters that I want to comment on in passing. One of the main features of the bill is a provision permitting banks to get into the whole field of mortgage lending. This is a good move and one which I think will meet with general acceptance. There are, however, one or two aspects of this which we should like to refer to the Minister for his consideration, so that when he appears as a willing witness we will be able to go into these matters with him in greater detail.
We suggest to him for his consideration that the limitation of three quarters of the value of property is too low, and that some consideration might be given to permitting the banks to lend up to something closer to the 90 per cent figure of the value of the property that is being put forward. We have had various legislative items permitting this so far as private lenders are concerned, and we think it advisable to extend it to the banks.
Second, the total limit of 1 per cent per year deposit liabilities, which in actual figures would be about $160 million per year which the banks could put into mortgages, seems to us to be much too low to permit the banks to become a very significant factor in mortgage financing in Canada. Broken down, this might account for about 10,000 housing units; and it seems to us, having regard to the increase in housing requirements as forecast by the Economic Council, consideration will have to be given to raising this limitation so that banks can play a proper, adequate and influential role.
Third, there should be a requirement that a sizeable amount of funds invested in mortgages should go to financing ordinary housing. What is really needed, as the Minister is well aware, coming from an urban area, is a constant source upon which the housing industry can rely for housing financing. Previous governments tended to regard housing financing as largely a pump priming operation in respect of employment opportunities.

June 14, 1965
Bank Act
We have never really had in the housing field a guarantee of a constant source of financing to which we could look, and this has to a large degree accounted for the imbalance in the whole housing picture. It seems to us that if there is a larger amount available, this will be of great assistance.
Fourth, some machinery should be set up for policing mortgage lending so that it will not be used merely to raise the level of interest which can be charged on business loans. In short, the banks should not be able to deem the real property put up as security on an otherwise commercial loan, just so it can charge more than 6 per cent.
We also suggest for consideration that the Government give some thought to the establishment of regulations to be put into the Bank Act so the banks cannot avoid the 6 per cent straight limitation by either adding on extra service charges, or demanding that borrowers keep certain minimum balances in their accounts. There is a lot in the Act about secondary reserves and cash reserves, but we should like to reserve our comment in that regard until a later date.
One important provision in the Act is the provision, inserted, I gather, at the insistence of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon), which will in effect prohibit Provincial Governments from owning shares in commercial banks, and certainly from exercising any degree of control over them. Personally, this is a subject in respect of which I am open to persuasion. The first thing we should like to emphasize is that in consideration of this whole problem, we are of the group which feels that nothing should be done to interfere with the ability of the Central Bank to effectively conduct the monetary and fiscal affairs of the country, and that anything which would detract from that would be unwise.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, I find it difficult at the moment to draw a distinction between the Act incorporating three Toronto financiers into a commercial bank, and permission for Provincial Governments, or the people of provinces through their elected Governments, to have the right to participate in a bank unless, as I have said, the Minister can show that there are other considerations which enter into this, and that the fact of a Provincial Government owning a bank or having a large degree of share participation in it, in some special way will enable that Government to persuade such a bank to interfere with Central Bank Policy. Of course all we have had to date is opinion evidence from the Minister. He has given us

bland assurances that this danger exists and that this legislation is necessary to overcome that danger. If the Minister can convince us that this is the case, again when he appears as a witness, we also suggest that he consider this proposition. If there are some such problems created by the special situation of a Provincial Government being involved in a bank, we might well in the committee consider whether the Bank Act could be so revised and strengthened as to overcome the danger. It might be better to direct our minds in this direction rather than to assume in the beginning that we should exclude Provincial Governments from any participation in banking activities.
As I have said, this is a very important principle of the bill. We are anxious to maintain the authority and prestige of the Central Bank and, at least for myself, we are open to persuasion on this particular aspect.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
The other matter we want to comment on in passing deals with the new method of incorporating banks. I am quite prepared to concede that the present system is certainly somewhat ridiculous in that private Members, rightly or wrongly, can band together and talk out these various bank charter bills. It seems an unwise way of incorporating some of our main financial institutions. But at the same time it seems to us, subject to clarification, that the new method also raises dangers.
We have heard a suggestion that new charters will be granted by the Cabinet and we want to suggest that this lays the Cabinet open to the same problem of improper influence and improper connections in the granting of charters. Rather than creating that danger, which I suggest is a real one, it seems to us that we should give consideration in the committee to revising the procedures by which the House grants charters so that small groups could not, as has been done in the past, effectively blockade such bills. Even though I have participated in some of these debates, I am prepared to admit it is not a proper procedure and that there ought to be some form of revision.
I think we do not want to comment any further at this time because, in keeeping with the new spirit of haste and co-operation evident under the new rules, we would like to get the bill to the committee. But I do want to repeat the suggestion I made in the beginning that the Government give the committee a thorough briefing. The only other suggestion I would ask the Minister to con-
June 14, 1965

sider is that he investigate whether or not some form of insurance of safety deposit boxes against robbery cannot be established. So many people have lost their holdings in the past, because of the lack of such protection, that we would like to see whether legislation cannot be devised so that safety deposit box holders can be protected by insurance against the risk of robbery. Other than that, Mr. Speaker, we tentatively support the bill and urge that it go to the committee for careful study.

Mr. Speaker, we too would like to see the bill go to the Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs before the summer recess, and along that line we support the notice of a further extension of existing bank charters given a few days ago by the Minister of Finance. We want to ask a number of questions when the bill is before the committee and with regard to most of the proposed changes we will withhold our remarks until that time.
I see that the hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) is still here, although he is near the curtain and not actually in the House. In his opening remarks he made the suggestion that I had been talking through my hat on a number of occasions with respect to the subject of banks and banking. I am not particularly interested, Mr. Speaker, in whether or not the hon. Member for Edmonton West agrees with me. What I said was that twice this Parliament has had to extend the charters of the existing banks because there was not sufficient time to deal with the required decennial revision of the Bank Act. He says now that I am talking through my hat because the report of the Porter Royal Commission was not even available to the House until February of 1964 and therefore it was impossible to do the necessary work in time to meet the deadline of June 30, 1964. It may be his opinion that there was not time, Mr. Speaker, but I suggest that if the Minister of Finance had not been preoccupied with getting his budget ready and a number of other very important duties it might have been possible for him and his department to prepare changes to the Bank Act and present them to Parliament before June, 1964. Possibly it might not have been, but what I said was that there is a requirement now that there be a deferment of two years. I stand by that, whether or not the hon. Member for Edmonton West agrees with me.
Bank Act
When it comes to talking through one's hat I think we all have to give the hon. Member for Edmonton West first prize because when the resolution preceding the bill was before the House on May 6 he said, as found on page 1001 of Hansard:
In so far as the Alberta Provincial Treasury Branches are concerned, certainly those of us who do not share the political views of the present administration in Alberta would like to see a great deal more light shed on their operations.
Then he went on to say:
The Provincial Treasurer merely brings in a record of the year's operations, showing either a loss or a profit. We do know that in the background there have been some rather odd things that have happened.
He went on to say that the report on the Treasury Branch system is never examined in committee, that the officers of the Alberta Treasury Branch system are not brought before a committee for examination, and so on. I have a letter here about this matter from the Provincial Treasurer of Alberta and this is what he says:
When the Public Accounts are being studied by the Public Accounts Committee of the Legislature at each session the members have every opportunity to ask all the questions they wish regarding the operation of the branches. At the 1965 session the opposition members asked that the committee give special attention to the branches, and several senior officials attended hearings of the committee until all questions had been exhausted and fully answered.
