speechtext:
If the hon. Member for Edmonton West had nothing constructive to say about the operations of the Alberta Treasury Branch system, I suggest he would have been better off to say nothing. The fact is that the Alberta Treasury Branch system is very popular. It is providing a service that is so much in demand throughout the Province that there is difficulty in keeping up with the demand for more and more branches. At the moment the limiting factor is the train-

June 14, 1965
Bank Act
ing of personnel to keep up with the expansion that is being demanded.
To get back to Bill No. C-102 now before us, when the Minister of Finance made his opening statement on second reading of the bill on May 18 he said a number of things that are of very great interest to the Members of this party, and I am going to try to go over them very briefly in the same order in which he mentioned them in his statement. With regard to monetary policy he referred to the absolute size, power, control and influence of our banking institutions. We agree with that statement, but because this is so we say that the Bank of Canada and the Department of Finance ought to exercise a very large degree of control over their operations so that the Government will in fact have effective control of the monetary policy of the country.
Another point the Minister made was that while the Porter Commission recommended that the Bank Act be changed to bring under the umbrella of that legislation near banks and other institutions performing essentially the same functions as our banks are, the Government was not prepared to accept and adopt this recommendation in its entirety at this time.
[DOT] (5:20 pm.)
Well, Mr. Speaker, we believe there are some rather large tasks ahead for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) if he is going to enact Federal legislation that will require all of these deposit taking institutions to be brought under the Bank Act. First of all, on May 18, the Minister sugested that a bank has not been clearly defined. He said, in fact, that there are several definitions of a bank at this time. In so far as the Federal Government was concerned, for the time being, they were going to more or less confine the provisions of the Bank Act to those institutions that were actually chartered by the Federal Government. I feel that is wise because of the tremendous implications inherent in an attempt to bring these near banks under the Bank Act, until we have a clearer definition.
The Minister did, however, say that at a later date there may be some other improvements made in the Bank Act, involving other recommendations by the Porter Commission. The Province of Alberta, I think, is a little apprehensive about this statement because if the Bank Act itself should be broadened to include deposit taking institutions in addition to the chartered banks in the near future, then of course we would like to know what

further action the Government proposes to take in the direction of achieving these directives. We hope there will be sufficient discussion between the Federal and Provincial Governments, and perhaps in the committee that is to study this bill, so that more light will be thrown on the further action the Government intends to take. The Minister did not spell out how much further the Government intended to go. He did not say they were going to do it in this session, as a matter of fact. This is the reason for the apprehension, because he did indicate the Government intended to go farther at a later date.
In so far as allowing the banks to go into the conventional mortgage field is concerned and allowing the banks to charge what is referred to as the going rate of interest, which could be 1 per cent or 2 per cent above the 6 per cent limit, we do not have any serious disagreement with that. We feel there is a need in Canada for larger amounts of mortgage money to keep the pace of building going, in order to provide homes of a higher standard for Canadians. We agree wholeheartedly with the Minister's statement that the Government is not going to change the 6 per cent limit on interest rates during this revision of the Bank Act. The Minister stated also, as reported on page 1430 of Hansard for May 18, that it was the Government's desire, in fact it was the Government's policy to keep interest rates as low as possible. He suggested, too, that if they had allowed an increase from 6 per cent to any figure above that, there could have been an immediate increase in the rate of interest to small businesses. I agree with that statement. I am not sure that I agree the Government has done all of those things it ought to have done to keep interest rates as low as possible.
It seems to me it is unnecessary for the Federal Government to be offering substantially over 5 per cent rate of interest on its own Government bonds. After all, these offerings that are made by the Minister of Finance can be considered as prime interest rates, and other interest rates move in relationship to what the Department of Finance allows on these Government bonds. These bonds are certainly prime, gilt edged securities. I am pleased to note that according to the advertisement in today's newspapers Government offerings are at perhaps a slightly lower rate of interest. The offerings on a ten months basis are going to be at 3.5 per cent; the ones for 11 months at 4.5 per cent, and the one for a year at 5 per cent. I believe those rates are slightly less than some
June 14, 1965

of the previous issues. If there is a trend in this direction, I am pleased to see it.
The Minister referred also to the fact that there is a wider dispersal of the ownership of the shares of the chartered banks. This might be the case, but I believe the actual controlling interest in the eight chartered banks is not so widely dispersed as the Minister would like Members of this House to believe. I say that, because there are some trust and loan companies that have been set up and which hold very large blocks of the voting stock of chartered banks. Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, these same trust and loan companies have large portions of their own stock held by banks. I am pleased to note the Minister said the Government is going to take some action to do away with these interlocking directorships between these trust companies and the chartered banks.
I have some charts before me which indicate there are large blocks of bank stock owned by certain trust companies and, in turn, the same banks own controlling stock of some trust companies. This is something therefore that the Government needs to look into very carefully. I just do not accept the argument that the small shareholders of the chartered banks in Canada have any say whatever in the policies being followed by these banks. It is these blocks of votes, even if they only amount to 10 per cent, that more or less control the policies of the banks. There have been times when I believe the banks have not had their fingers on the pulse of Canada; they have not adopted policies to meet the credit demands of the rank and file of Canadians.
We know that the banks have now moved into the field of small loans, term loans and so on. This has been very useful. Prior to the banks taking this action, they fail to recognize and meet the very legitimate demands for small loans, personal loans, term loans and things of that nature. The result was that there was a tremendous expansion of these small, consumer finance companies and they were allowed to charge exorbitant interest rates. I think it is well for the banks to move into this field and to be very aggressive in picking up this business, so we do not have these loan sharks doing the kind of business they have been doing over the past few years. I hope there will be other provisions, and that there will be some teeth in them, so that there will be a wide disposal of bank shares, and furthermore that something will be done to make sure that the
Bank Act
actual control of these banks is not restricted to an ever smaller group of people.
We note also that the annual reports of the chartered banks in Canada from now on will have to contain a great deal more information than they have in the past. This is something that is long overdue.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
I note from an article in the Financial Post of May 15 that:
Canada's chartered banks, whose annual reports have long been the despair of financial analysts, will have to provide more information to their shareholders if the Government's Bank Act changes are passed.
I have the reports of the Bank of Montreal, the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce and several others in front of me. In all of them invariably some kind of figure is put down for profit, but it always goes something like this-"After transfers to inner reserves." If you look at these reports carefully sometimes you can find what the provision may be for taxes and depreciation, but you can never find out how much they transfer to the inner reserves. Then there is another figure below that which shows the net profit, or the amount to be distributed by way of dividends after transfers from the inner reserves."
As a matter of fact, up until now several of the figures in these bank reports have left one knowing less about their operations after reading them than before. Therefore I hope the new provisions will make mandatory the disclosure of a number of things. From now on it appears that a bank's annual financial statement will have to show the income it gets from loans, from other securities, and the amount involved in operating revenue. Thus there will be a greater breakdown of revenue than has been shown in the past, and as expenses there will be shown interest on deposits, salaries, property tax and other operating expenses. From all this, it will be possible to get a far clearer picture of the operation of banks than we have had in the past.
Concern has been expressed about the matter of provincial governments owning stock, especially common stock, in a chartered bank. There will be a difficult constitutional problem here because in essence the Federal Government is telling the provinces that they cannot invest their funds in that kind of security. Whether the Federal Government has authority to do so is questionable, but it seems to me that the influence, in fact the control that the Federal Government can exercise on the operations of the chartered banks

June 14, 1965
Bank Act
through the Bank of Canada is sufficient, so that there would be no transfer of responsibility for monetary policy, despite who owns the common stock.
If the Minister of Finance argues that by allowing provincial governments to own common stock in banks they may be able to have an undue influence on national monetary policy, that is tantamount to arguing that the present shareholders in chartered banks could, if they wished, have a tremendous effect on national monetary policy. He cannot have it both ways. Either the present shareholders do in fact have a tremendous influence and do in fact exercise that influence on our national monetary policy, or else there is no danger in provincial governments owning this stock.
I personally believe that the provisions of the Bank Act, even as it exists today, are sufficient to retain full and complete authority over monetary policy in the hands of the Federal Government, and I do not accept the argument that there is any inherent danger in the provincial governments owning such stock.
In the case of British Columbia, in that rapidly growing industrial complex out on the west coast, it would be beneficial to that area to have a bank with its head office there, so that it would have particular concern for the industrial and commercial expansion of that area. What is more, I believe that if the provincial government were to subscribe part of the stock, be it 10 per cent or even less, it would give to other investors in such a bank the kind of confidence and assurance needed to make sure it succeeds. I think the Minister must agree that all the Premier of B.C. asked for was authority to buy 10 per cent or less of the common stock. In my opinion that is not an unreasonable request.
In Alberta, when the Alberta Gas Trunk Line was being incorporated and when Great Canadian Tar Sands was being incorporated the provincial government insisted that the shares be first offered to Alberta residents, and that was sufficient inducement to make certain both issues were tremendously oversubscribed. By having some kind of endorsa-tion from a provincial government it seems to add to the success of this kind of operation.
We will have an opportunity to discuss many of these matters in the committee. I hope that before the end of the week the Minister will introduce the bill to extend the bank charters for a further period. On this occasion he is asking for an extension of

six months. I think the committee might be finished within six months, but it might be just as well for the Minister to ask for a little longer extension in the event that committee discussions and investigations take longer than he anticipates at present. If the Minister wishes, we would be willing to extend the charters for a year. In such case the committee would be under no pressure whatever. It would be able to call all the witnesses it wanted and take all the time it felt necessary to debate and investigate the matter.
Though the charters be extended for a year I would hope the committee could finish its work by the end of 1965. I do not propose to speak any longer on this bill, since it is going to committee and since there will be a second bill to extend the charters for a further period.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)

subtopic: DECENNIAL REVISION AND EXTENSION OF CHARTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the legislation under study, Bill C-102, allowing banks to carry on business for a further ten years, cannot be treated lightly, and this, on account of its significance, since the future of the economic blood of the nation is in question.
However, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) seems quite in a hurry; he would like this bill to be quickly referred to the committee on banking and commerce.
For more than 30 years now we have been fighting the present financial system. We are asking the Minister of Finance to be patient, because we wish to show him that the present banking system must be reformed from the ground up, and not only by means of minor amendments which, finally, would allow the banks to increase their wealth.
In his remarks, the Minister spoke about the cash reserve percentage the banks shall maintain with the Bank of Canada.
That is precisely the greatest imbalance of the banking system.
I should have liked the Minister to give us a description or to draw us a picture of the banking system.
At the same time that would have opened the eyes of many members of the house who do not understand the present system.
Since the Minister did not do so, I should like to make a few remarks now.
Today, in all civilized countries, there exists an institution whose function is to issue money. Such an institution is called a bank.
June 14. 1965

Since the beginning of the pastoral era- and even nowadays-exchange can be reduced to barter. The use of a third commodity which divides barter into sale and purchase is resorted to for utilitarian purposes.
If a farmer wanted to exchange a horse for bread, he could obviously not exchange his horse for the minimum quantity of bread required daily. He would therefore issue to the baker some leather tokens or any other conventional token of a certain value.
The baker would demand the horse when he would be in possession of a certain amount of tokens. This currency would be a means of exchange on settlement of a different quantity and quality of various goods. Money would be as it is today, a promise to pay in kind on request.
One is immediately aware that currency was then issued according to the production needs, the commodities and services to be exchanged. In other words, a person who disposed or hoped to dispose of $10 worth of goods could issue, at different intervals, $10 worth of money, while promising to pay in goods or services the party from whom he purchased goods or services.
At that time production did not issue currency under the form of an interest bearing loan, but normally under the form of a promise to render services for an appraised value equal to the services rendered.
There is only one step to take in order that this type of currency might be legal tender recognized by the state. The authorities, the government or the state, aware through its statistical services of the volume of production required to meet consumer needs, can issue a volume of currency equal to that production.
The state can issue currency and commit itself to reimburse its value to the people; such currency can circulate freely and be used as an instrument of exchange.
The issuing of money will keep pace with consumption and new issues will be made to meet requirements as production increases.
While today money is issued by private organizations as debts to producers, money must be issued by the state, without interest, directly to consumption and in sufficient quantity to buy goods and services produced.
We can therefore conclude with this definition of money: a means of exchange invented by man to exchange products and services against an equal value in products and services under the control and guaranty of the state.
22620-150J
Bank Act
In the circumstances the banker is in a unique position. He is probably the only man able to lend money without giving away anything and to make a profit on the transaction, since in the first place he gets his merchandise without cost.
What is the present machinery for creating credit? Here is an example:
Since the machinery by which money is created by the banks, is not generally understood, and since that subject is of course of the utmost importance, it would be a good idea to repeat what the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) said during the debate on the resolution.
Let us take the case of a bank being formed; its social capital is immaterial. Ten depositors make a $100 deposit each in treasury bonds in that bank. Its responsibility toward the public amounts then to $1,000.
Those ten depositors do business with one another and find it more convenient, in many cases, to write notes or cheques to the banker informing him to adjust their account according to those business operations, rather than withdrawing each time legal currency to make their own payments.
After a short while the banker notices that only 8 per cent, or thereabouts, of his business is handled in legal tender-and today, according to the minister's statement, it seems that the percentage will be reduced to 7 per cent, since he tells us that hereafter the cash reserve will be 7 per cent.
As I was saying, the banker has noticed that only 8 per cent, or thereabouts, of his business was handled in legal tender, all the rest being mere bookkeeping entries. I am still talking about today's credit machinery.
At that time depositor No. 10, who is a manufacturer, receives an order. Before delivering the goods, he finds he will have to pay in wages, salaries and other expenses, far more money than is available to him.
Faced with this difficulty, he consults his banker who, after considering the above-mentioned situation, agrees to let him withdraw from his account, not only his own $100, but $100 more, a total of $200, in consideration of payment, within three months, of $106.
Such an overdraft of $100 is a credit in the account of depositor No. 10 who can now draw $200.
The responsibilities of the banker toward the public now amount to $1,100; none of the original depositors had their deposit reduced

June 14, 1965
Bank Act
in the process nor were they consulted on this matter and it is quite correct to say that $100 worth of new money has been created with a stroke of the pen. Depositor No. 10, having fortunately secured his overdraft, distributes it to his employees in the form of salaries.
All the costs are included in the price the public pays for products and, consequently, when depositor No. 10 repays his banker with the $106 obtained from the public in exchange for the products, the banker, having placed in his profit and loss account the $6 of interest priorly created by him, compares the $100 received against the apparent credit priorly created and cancels both of them.
There is $100 worth more goods immobilized for which nobody, not even the banker, except potentially, has the equivalent in money.
Money, under its various forms, in bank or credit notes, as long as they are convertible, was defined by Professor Walker in his book entitled Money, Trade and Industry, as any medicine which has been accepted to such an extent that, no matter what it contains, no matter why the public wants it, nobody refuses it as a means of exchange for products.
As long as this definition holds, it is obvious that the possession of money or credit notes which are convertible establishes a direct link with services of others in direct proportion to the fraction of total stock controlled and, furthermore, the total financial wealth in the world, including credit, should, according to this definition, suffice to balance the total book values, material assets and potential production of the world.
Few people would think that monetary systems established in the world are perfect, and the number of those people is decreasing every day.
But when you ask for a definition of the various faults of the monetary system, it is interesting to note how the ideas of justice and value are referred to with monotonous regularity.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
Possibly the most important basic idea which may be advanced at this time, as regards the monetary system, is that money is not in a true sense a measure of values.
The proper function of the monetary system is to serve through the exchange and distribution of goods and services.
It is, or should be, a system of order and not a system of rewards.

It is essentially an administrative system subjected to politics, and because it is above all other administrative systems, the international control of currency is extremely important.
To correct the situation created by the present banking system, a technique must be found to adjust, by means of credit, and to create a relationship between the average level of prices and the available purchasing power. Under present conditions, the banking system is responsible for making that adjustment.
Finance and taxation, nowadays, are but an ingenious system for the concentration of financial power.
One could say that almost any explanation that does not completely and accurately describe how the financial system operates has the curious effect of helping the supporters of the system.
If you take the system as a whole, it seems obvious that, sooner or later, the monopoly exercised by the powers of finance must be attacked and that taxes, far from attacking it, are doing a great deal toward consolidating its powers.
What do the Creditistes propose to improve the present banking system? Here is a brief description of a reform we are advocating.
The financial system is but a system of notes that should reflect the realities of production and not control them. Finance should assist industry and business and not dominate them. The means now available to produce wealth were created by geniuses and inventors now gone to their reward and they belong to everybody and everybody ought to benefit from the results of those inventions, because they represent the greatest factor of production there is today.
Therefore, it is a factor from which all should benefit equally.
But no drastic reform will be possible as long as credit and the banking system are controlled by the persons who now dominate them.
It must follow that a national authority, representing the people, should regain control of credit and of the financial system which now constitutes a monopoly in the hands of chartered banks. We already have that authority. It is the Bank of Canada.
To reform the system we must first of all resort to the following basic principles:
Money credits in the hands of the population must equal the sum of prices attached to consumer goods on sale, whatever those prices, and those money credits can only be recalled, rescinded or depreciated by the
June 14, 1965

purchase or the depreciation of these consumer goods.
The credits required to finance production must not come from savings, but from new credits issued for that production and they must be rescinded or recalled only in the proportion of the general depreciation with regard to general appreciation.
Distribution of monetary signs to individuals must become less and less dependant on employment. This means that the dividend will progressively replace salaries and wages as the man-hour production increases.
Thus, the following steps become necessary:
The setting up of a national accounting
system;
The setting up of an agency to create the necessary new credits;
The distribution of a national dividend to allow everyone to benefit from applied science and to solve the problems of automation and unemployment; this technique would finally be rounded out by the application of a compensated discount intended to maintain the equilibrium between the monetary signs and the available goods and services.
Now, let us turn to the new credit. At the present time any new credit is issued by the chartered banks which lend new credits to producers at a certain interest.
The new credit required for the financing of production should not be supplied by savings, but by new credit issued for this production. This new credit must be cancelled or recalled only in the proportion of the general depreciation to the general appreciation. Therefore, new credit must be used to mobilize industry toward new production. At first sight, the banks are the proper agencies to fill this role and grant the necessary credit toward production. But contrary to the situation which exists at this moment, this credit would not belong to them but to every citizen.
The Bank of Canada, the issuing bank, an agency of the government and of the people, would grant banks the necessary credit as industry required it. Moreover, banks are well equipped to play this part. They have branches everywhere, and well trained personnel able to evaluate local needs as well as the credit rating of borrowers.
For the service they would provide, surely banks should be entitled to a reward, a payment allowing them to discharge their responsibilities. Those credits could be obtained
Bank Act
at nominal cost from the Bank of Canada or at some other interest rate.
But banks should not demand a higher rate from borrowers. The increase of real credit caused by the increase of production would allow the Bank of Canada, by levying a part of this surplus to pay the banks for services rendered. And if banks refuse to act as agents of the community they should be forced to do so; refractory bankers should be replaced.
What is the function of chartered banks?
At present chartered banks can multiply their credit by 12.5, taking as a basis all the deposits they hold such as treasury bills and Canada bonds.
We therefore propose that the privilege of banks to multiply credit by 12.5 for their benefit be abolished and that they only be authorized to lend their own assets, especially the shareholders' investments, the deposits of small investors, to buy consumer goods or for personal purposes. What would be the result of such a policy?
I would like to point out that at the present time, according to the report of the Porter Commission, non financial companies had borrowed at the end of 1960, $2,901 million from banks and moreover, at the end of 1961, chartered banks were holding $470 million worth of company bonds.
Now, at the end of that same year, chartered banks held $3,371 million worth of Canada bonds, that is exactly the same amount invested by the banks in Canadian companies through bank loans or the purchase of their bonds. It is obvious that if the Canadian government redeemed its bonds held by banks, the latter would dispose of an equal amount for industrial or commercial loans.
We maintain that chartered banks could keep on granting loans but for personal purposes or the purchase of consumer goods. And if this currency proved insufficient, as is to be expected, the Bank of Canada would be authorized to make advances to chartered banks so that they might have available the necessary liquid assets to meet personal needs.
Now, if we consider social development, we notice that social needs, social development of the country, the building of roads, bridges, canals, waterworks, sidewalks, schools, hospitals, libraries, are financed by private capital, which deprives industries needing money for their development of the necessary capital and forces them sometimes
*2356

June 14, 1965
Bank Act
to seek it in foreign countries. This places our economy under foreign domination.
If the development or building of fiscal capital in our country were financed by new credit issued on behalf of society by the Bank of Canada or local banks at a nominal interest cost, by using the real credit of the country, this capital advanced by the Bank of Canada, at administrative costs, to finance the social development of the country, would not remain indefinitely in circulation and would be recalled at the depreciation rate of this social capital, thus eliminating the danger of inflation.
The issuance of this new credit would be made in relation to the needs for schools, hospitals, and so on.
National needs, actual needs, determine and regulate the scrip money projected by anticipation.
And this new money, this new credit should not bear interest, because it is used to build social capital which is non-profitable.
Such are the various methods suggested to put into force the Creditiste philosophy to ensure always a satisfactory balance between production and demand.
Those are, Mr. Speaker, the changes needed to reform the monetary system which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) should have presented to us if he really wanted the government to have a definite monetary policy and to control absolutely the creation of credit in Canada.

subtopic: COMMISSION TO REPORT ON A NATIONAL TRAINING SERVICE PROGRAM
COMMISSION TO REPORT ON A NATIONAL TRAINING SERVICE PROGRAM
speechtext:
That, In the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of undertaking a searching study of the youth problem in Canada, paralleling the possibility of setting up in the country a "National Training Service" for young people between the ages of 18 and 21 years, and
That, to this end, there should be appointed a Commission made up of representatives of the various bodies concerned with health, education, employment, and the Armed Forces, charged with reporting to this House on the advantages and
June 14, 1965	COMMONS
disadvantages of such a "National Training Service", particularly with regard to the following points:
1.	Discipline and respect for our institutions and for authority.
2.	The possibility of its complementing training and education.
3.	Improvement in health through physical education.
4.	A means of promoting bilingualism among the young.
5.	Strengthening of national unity through better knowledge of the country and its various ethnic groups.
6.	Co-ordination with the Emergency Measures Organization.
7.	Advantages in the Service being run by the Armed Forces or other similar body.
8.	Possible duration of such a service and particular application to students.
He said: Mr. Speaker, if I have introduced again this year, a new notice of motion concerning the setting up in this country of a National Training Service, it is because I am more convinced than ever that various benefits would be derived from such a decision on the part of the government, more so even, since the months gone by have enabled me to find out that Canadians as a whole, as well as the people from the province of Quebec, favour most the establishment in this country of such a national service for our young people.
Mr. Speaker, at this point, may I digress a moment to add that during the last 12 months, I have continually received correspondence from various persons across the country. Furthermore, during the year the French speaking Junior Chambers of Commerce of Canada have chosen as the theme for their annual debating contest: "Compulsory military service, for or against". The final contest will take place on July 2, at the Chateau Fron-tenac, in Quebec City. It is nevertheless significant to find that people are interested in discussing this matter.
During the debate last year, I found that too much emphasis was laid on the words "compulsory military service" or on the word "conscription"; and the same thing can be said about the publicity made through our media of information.
That is why I have elected this year to introduce my notice of motion in a completely different manner so that, by listing a few particular points to be considered, the most obvious advantages may be seen immediately. Furthermore, I wish to point out at the outset to the hon. members of the house that the motion now before us is not
DEBATES	2357
National Training Service asking the government to institute immediately such a service, but rather to suggest the appointment of a commission to examine all its implications and the advantages which may be derived therefrom.
Personally, I am convinced that such military training should come under the jurisdiction of the armed forces, but I thought I should leave the door open to other suggestions and that is why I suggest that representatives of groups of people interested in health, education, employment, the armed forces and, I would even add, social, rehabilitation and welfare services, should sit on that study commission.
Mr. Speaker, parents and educators are increasingly concerned about the future of our youth; and there is even apprehension in the minds of many of them. I would not want to give the impression of being an alarmist, a bogey-man and I am not saying either that there is no solution to the youth problem, but as head of a family I wonder about many things. I wonder about the same things which are bothering most parents, and I am trying to see what the future has in stock; I wonder what is lacking both within the family and our education system.
Some will say that youth must have its fling; others will add that we have all had ours. But do you not agree with me that we are nevertheless increasingly concerned about this unrestrained and free-thinking attitude?
Is this normal, this lack of respect for elders, this contempt for established authority and this tendency to do away with everything? It is disturbing to see how new doctrines and theories often talk about liberty as meaning licence and how basic democratic principles joining together liberty and responsibility are ignored.
You might say: "But what does a national training service have to do with all that?" Don't you fear, I do not think the creation of such a service would muzzle our youth in a discipled body where there would be no possibility of dialogue and where militarism would be used to crush the rebels. However, you know it is becoming always more vital to keep our young people busy, to allow them to know all the aspects of our society and to make them appreciate the things they often take for granted.
Many Canadians agree that a form of national service would constitute a wonderful instrument for helping our youth to develop both physically and intellectually in a dis-
2358	COMMONS DEBATES	June 14, 1965
National Training Service ciplined environment, giving them a sense ol values and respect for our institutions and for authority.
In a speech he made recently, His Excellency the Governor General of Canada expressed his regret that frontiers sometimes took on the aspect of barriers rather than meeting places. He invited people to open wide the provincial doors and windows, to look beyond the walls at what is going on outside.
"Let us become acquainted", he said, "because that is how we will learn to understand each other." He even suggested massive group travels between provinces in order to improve mutual understanding.
That is one of my main points, Mr. Speaker, in stating the advantages of the national training service in Canada, that is a means to enable our youth to know Canada and to visit the various areas of the country. I think it would be very beneficial to split such a service stage into four three-month periods so that the young men could alternately visit in the Maritimes, in the Eastern provinces, in the Prairies and finally on the Pacific Coast. To know one's country is to have exchanges with all those who live in it and in order to achieve this, I see nothing better than to use that national service as the most efficient school of language for young Canadians. The program could be organized in such a way that there would be a certain continuity as much in terms of education as in terms of physical training or anything else.
To those who would fear an interference from the federal government in the field of education-

Mr. Speaker, so far as I am concerned, I am quite agreeable to letting the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) go, if he is that weak and cannot attend the debate.
Resuming my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I say to those who would fear interference by the federal government in the field of education that I have no objection to this being done in co-operation with the provinces. In my view, surely there is a way to preserve provincial autonomy while at the same time, co-ordinating efforts of the greatest advantage to our young people. One thing that has not been mentioned in the various points suggested for study is the possibility of relating to such an institution a world history course, and what may be even more important, a Canadian history course.
Speaking for myself, I feel that the best presently available vehicle toward that end is none other than the Department of National Defence; still, I remain open to any suggestion and would even be willing to see the government set up a body within which the various interested parties could work in co-operation with the Departments of Health, of Labour and of National Defence.
June 14, 1965	COMMONS
This agency, which I called in my notice of motion "National Training Service" could bear any other name; I might even suggest that of "Canadian Youth Service".
At the very time when a program is being launched with a view to creating a Company of Young Canadians, it seems to me we would be shirking our responsibilities by failing to give to the government this wonderful opportunity of making a comprehensive study of the youth problem in Canada. Let us set aside the bugaboo of conscription, let us forget momentarily military questions and the shadow of war, and let us study the whole problem in the Canadian context, with a view to fostering national unity, as a means to better training, better understanding and good will.
I would like to point out clearly my views as regards the objection of those who claim that all this would be detrimental to the educational program of our youth and could make them lose a year's studies. In my opinion, it is easy to settle this problem by not compelling anyone to complete his 12 months of service before he has completed his studies, for those who wish to do so at the secondary level after their technical studies. It would be advisable for those who pursue university studies or who specialize beyond secondary school, to complete the service by three month stages, during their holidays and over a period of three or four years. Thus every young Canadian would enjoy the same advantages-and I mean "advantages" because I sincerely believe in it, and no one could upbraid the government for having delayed his studies or hampered his future.
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to venture too far today in regard to the cost of this project, but I feel that there are enough advantages to justify such a government expenditure. I want to correct some statements made last year in this house with respect to a tremendous amount, which was far from reality.
Certainly, it would be in order to pay the young people in service a reasonable allowance which could compare to the amount a new recruit gets now, or at least $20 a week, that is a total of $1,000 for 12 months. On the basis of this amount of $1,000 and considering that the number of young Canadians in service each year would be 100,000,
I arrived last year at a maximum cost of $300 million, including maintenance and administrative expenditures, instructors and specialized staff. I did not invent those figures 22620-151

National Training Service myself, and I can assure you that they are close enough to reality, and that it is perhaps possible to reduce them to $250 million.
It is true that here I do not take into consideration capital expenditures which should normally and gradually be incurred, especially if one considers that it would be advisable to erect, through the years, centres similar to our military colleges with permanent buildings which, by the same token, are much more attractive and help to create an atmosphere more suitable to study and training.

Although they would be expensive, those centres would always remain available to the government in case of conflict or emergency. Since this national service could easily make up for the militia and the armed forces reserve, almost $40 million would be saved each year and which would provide a substantial amount for the establishment of such a building program.
Last year some people were shocked when I said that this would also help to solve the problem of unemployment. I will not mention here some of the political arguments which were used, but I will say only: Can you deny the fact that such a project would free the labour market of 100,000 people, an equivalent of $150 million in unemployment insurance benefits? Personally, I would rather see this amount spent in a constructive way instead of paying people to do nothing.
Mr. Speaker, I would have much to say on the possibilities of such a national training service; the more I discuss the matter with people, the more arguments are put forward in favour of such a scheme, and the more I am convinced that we would do our country a great service by passing that resolution. I, therefore, appeal to all the members of the House to consider favourably my proposal and at least allow it to come to a vote before the end of this discussion.

The hon. member has made another try this year and introduced again a proposal that is not clear, even in his own mind. He is ready to give to such a project any name whatever, provided his proposal is adopted.
One fact in particular strikes me-though it is true that this proposal is his own; he suggests that this plan be implemented in co-operation with the provinces. I cannot help making the following remark, namely that it is a surprising thing to see such a project being proposed during this session when it has been suggested that the provinces should withdraw from many joint programs. While we are endeavouring to withdraw from joint programs, the hon. member is introducing a motion in order to emphasize another one.
I would not like to be unpleasant to my hon. friend, but the reason why he is coming back this year with an entirely amended project is that last year, following his "conscription" project, since he used the word himself, or "compulsory military training", there were some feelings of unrest and some objections which surely attracted his atten-

tion. He may have secured support from some people in certain quarters, but as regards newspapers, their remarks were diametrically opposed to the opinion of the hon. member, who referred to unqualified encouragement on the part of the people with whom he got in touch with the exception of a few.
I know that a number of young people of his constituency have expressed to him, rather clearly and conclusively, their objections to that proposal, and he is probably seeking a way out by submitting a completely new and different project from that of last year.
The remarks of my hon. friend have made me realize that he did not exactly know what he would like to propose. He did not even have a clear idea of what he wanted, and that is why he tried to enlist the aid of all members in this House to put his proposal through.

I have always contended that we should have a federal bureau of education or department of education, not to provide education but to provide co-ordination and equality of educational opportunities across the country. The hon. Member has taken this into consideration because he has said his proposal would provide employment in such a field.
I have always believed that if we are to have an effective national unemployment insurance office, particularly an effective employment commission, we must set standards that will enable the Federal Government to provide equal opportunities for retraining the unemployed in all parts of Canada. This has not been possible in the technical field to date, and I think the hon. Member probably has in mind that the solution of technical education is a national problem. I believe the Federal Government should establish a national educational code in the technical field, and for that reason I think the hon. Member has made a very worth-while suggestion. However, I doubt if the Government will consider it at length.
We can look back at the compulsory training program we had a few years ago. People were violently opposed to it, even though it was an emergency program, and I can foresee reluctance on the part of many Members to support such a type of program.

worse before it improves. One reason for this is the large number of young people who are prepared to take on similar employment on a permanent basis.

I hope the motion will get speedy consideration in this House and that the Government will undertake to give leadership in bringing about a study of this type in the interest of providing increased opportunities for these young people who are finding it increasingly difficult to obtain employment.

There is no power to bring any of the officers of the system before a committee of the legislature. There is no committee examination, and there has not been any committee examination of the operations of the Provincial Treasury Branches.

June 14, 1965
Bank Act
That is absolutely wrong. The hon. Member was talking off the top of his hat. He may think he can justify his vagueness by such claims, but that is a sheer departure from the fact and he has not given correct information to this House. If he examined the 1955 report of the Public Accounts of the Province of Alberta, he would find that a committee dealt at length with the Treasury Branches and questioned the administrative heads of those branches. The only restriction placed on the question was the refusal to give public information in respect of individual accounts or loans. This is a practice followed by every chartered bank, the Porter Royal Commission and what we have known as the Banking and Commerce Committee of the House of Commons. Full particulars of the operation of the Treasury Branches are contained in the Alberta Public Accounts each year.
The services performed by the Treasury Branches of Alberta are not only in the field of banking, but also in the field of Government service generally, and these services were summarized by the Minister of Finance of Alberta in his first budget speech delivered to the Alberta Legislature a few months ago. I do not intend to deal with this at great length, but I think the record must be set straight.
The Alberta Public Accounts indicate that the Alberta Provincial Treasury Branches- and this was substantiated in the budget speech of the Minister himself-last year held a total value of deposits of $109,507,000. Total loans amounted to $65,873,000 with a total reserve for doubtful accounts as at March 31, 1964, of $3,388,000. I believe those figures indicate that these Treasury Branches are rendering a very important service to the public and to the commercial operations of that province. They also indicate a need for an extension of bank services presently being rendered to the people of Western Canada.
I do not understand the Minister of Finance in his action against Provincial Government investment in banks, and I refer not only to the application by British Columbia for a chartered bank, but to others, in view of the fact that the Governments of the provinces concerned are anxious that adequate banking facilities and services be provided to meet the needs of their citizens. For those reasons we support the applications for charters for the Bank of Western Canada and the Lauren tide Bank, as we will support others which indicate that they meet the requirements of the Bank Act.

Referring again to the legislation now before us, I should like again to state that it is significant more for what it does not contain than for what it does contain.
There are several points upon which we should like to commend the Minister. We commend him first of all for permitting an increase in the interest rate beyond 6 per cent for certain type of loans, which banks are presently not allowed to make. We commend him second, for bringing under the provisions of the Act some financial institutions, including near banks. I think this is necessary if we are going to have a financial policy on a national level. We also commend him for not tampering with credit unions or the Treasury Branches in Alberta, because we believe that both these institutions provide services which are essential to the economy and that they should be permitted to operate in this way. I trust there will be no attempt to deal with these matters either by amendment to the Bank Act or by secondary legislation such as the legislation dealing with the Quebec Savings Banks. Certain of these matters, of course, come within the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces and any attempt to curtail or circumvent provincial jurisdiction can expect to meet with strong resistance from the provinces.
[DOT] (7:10 p.m.)
Thus certain features of this new banking legislation appear to be improvements. Others are of questionable value. Information will undoubtedly be obtained when the bill goes before the committee, and we hope we may get through with this stage of our discussions tonight. The hearings of the Finance Committee would in my opinion be very important, and certainly as a result a lot of information is going to be brought to light. Therefore I would concur with my colleague, the hon. Member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson), in hoping that the Minister will not delay the introduction of the legislation to extend further the present Bank Act, and at the same time I do not see why there should be any reason to shorten the length of time of that postponement. Let us have enough time so we can consider these things in the depth in which I think they should be considered.
However, there are certain features of the new Bank Act that we might discuss at this stage. For instance, there is the provision with respect to the cash reserve requirement in clause 72, subclause 1. It requires a bank to maintain a cash reserve in the form of notes of and deposits with the Bank of
June 14, 1965

Canada. Subclause 3, however, authorizes the Bank of Canada to require a bank to maintain a secondary reserve in the form of notes of and deposits with the Bank of Canada as well as other types of secondary securities. Why should a bank be required to maintain a cash reserve and then a secondary cash reserve, both in the form of notes of and deposits with the Bank of Canada? Could not the Bank of Canada under this type of provision defeat the very purpose of the provision in clause 78 (2) whereby the cash reserve percentage of 8 per cent shall be decreased progressively to 7 per cent?
There seems to be no sound reason at all to abandon the power to maintain a flexible cash reserve ration for the banking system, even though this power has not been fully used for some time. This clause institutes a new secondary reserve system of treasury bill holdings in addition to the 7 per cent cash ratio reserve also required. It is putting into law what has been done unofficially for some years. Nevertheless, I do not quite see the purpose that the Minister has in mind in introducing this into the legislation. Why could we not have carried on under the present practice?
From the point of view of the stability of the banking system it may be a good thing but, of course, John Q. Public is having to pay the interest on the treasury bills that the banks have to hold. I repeat that some similar requirements to this and relating to cash reserve ratios should really be required of any institution that is actually engaged in some form of banking, that is, in the acceptance of deposits which are trans-ferrable and repayable on demand, but not backed 100 per cent by legal tender.
There are other questions to which we might refer that are not answered in this legislation. For instance, what about the relationship between a bank and a wholly owned trust company subsidiary? The legislation makes some reference to this and it seems that it is rather effective in one direction; but is this arrangement to be terminated or is it going to be allowed to continue? If so, under what terms and conditions will it be allowed to continue, keeping in mind that the Porter Commission made no recommendation as to banks being allowed to enter into the trust business at the present time, although it did recommend that the Bank Act be applied to a wider group of deposit taking institutions, which would seemingly include trust companies.
Bank Act
Section 18 (1) also raises a point of particular interest. This allows the bank to open accounts in central banks abroad and to accept deposits from central banks in other countries and pay interest on them. I may be reading too much into this, Mr. Speaker, but I believe this could develop into a most valuable instrument to aid international trade and settlements. In fact, I found it of particular interest because it is very similar to the recommendations made in a private Member's bill recently sponsored by my colleague, the hon. Member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Cote), which would amend the Bank of Canada Act to allow that bank to hold nonconvertible currencies of other nations in its reserves. If this is what the new legislation intends, I think we could very well find the answer to many of our problems that are related to international trade and settlements, and certainly it might be used to expand our trade beneficially from the point of view of financing the sale of many of our surplus commodities.
Appropriate Bank of Canada deposits of dollars with countries abroad, or accepting deposits of "soft" currencies in Canada could make it not too difficult to stabilize currencies of nations needing such help, and at the same time provide funds with which to develop trade with many of the emerging countries. In my opinion the question of aid is not just something related to dollars or technical know-how such as we have in great abundance in Canada, but such action would help in a very material way to facilitate trade between Canada and some of the emerging countries which desperately need such trade.
There is another very interesting section which I might mention briefly. I refer to section 23, which is actually repealed. An honourable funeral is here given to the myth that the value of our currency is in any way determined by its convertibility into gold. I am reminded of a quotation. I do not know the author but certainly it applies here. This quotation states:
A fallacy prevalent yet
Is to think that the money we get
Is based upon gold.
It's not. What we hold Is deposit, created by debt.
Again, if possible hon. Members might be asked to ruminate on the question: If this be so, then what does back our currency, and why? This is a good question as we seek to understand what goes on in our own financial system and how our monetary system functions.

June 14, 1965
Bank Act
Our economic system has indicated tor some time that we are now tending to move toward an inflationary trend which may well need to be checked. I am going to quote a few paragraphs from an article entitled "Money Supply At New Peak" which appeared on the 18th of May. The article reads in part as follows:
...the money supply was $18,743 million as at May 5, a new high record. This figure was up $193 million for the week, widest weekly increase since the end of March. In the past year-
In the fiscal year 1964-65.
-the money supply has expanded by $1,691 million.
Apparently it was thought that the affluent situation of the economy in particular required this, but certainly it is a lot of new money to come into existence in one week.
The amount of coin held outside the chartered banks is shown as $232 million in the latest report, unchanged from the preceding week. The amount of paper money or notes amounted to $1,933 million, an increase of $44 million for the week.
It is interesting to note that on the same date the amount of notes held by the chartered banks was $405 million, so that the public held nearly five times as much in paper money as the banks did. Bank notes do not earn interest, and banks tend to keep their holdings of such paper money at a minimum consistent with their requirements. In the week ended May 5 their holdings of bank notes were reduced by $40 million.
[DOT] (7:20 p.m.)
Then, Mr. Speaker, the same article mentions that the chartered banks, on May 5, held $3,746 million in Government of Canada securities, Treasury Bills and other securities, only $58 million less than a year ago. The article mentions that, in addition, they held $1,186 million on provincial, municipal and corporate securities, or $20 million more than a year ago and that deposits in, and notes of the Bank of Canada amounted to $1,368 million or $122 million more than a year ago.
As has already been brought to the attention of the House, the Government picked up $75 million of the present issue of Treasury Bills which went on the market today. This all refers back to the statement I made during the Throne Speech debate, Mr. Speaker, with regard to the fact that the Bank of Canada today holds approximately 15 per cent of the national debt. This is something many of us do not realize. Nevertheless, on August 7 of last year the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) himself mentioned the fact and it is recorded on page 6552 of Hansard that these holdings comprised 14.6 per cent of the total Government securities outstanding on

June 30, 1964. He stated also that the total income of the bank was $127,851,000 and the net income paid to the Consolidated Revenue Fund was $116,386,000. We are not protesting these facts. We are just pointing out that on this basis there is no reason why the Bank of Canada could not hold more of Canada's net debt, particularly since it is borne out that this is the policy of the present Government at this time. In other words, the Canadian people get the profit from the issues of this credit against their real credit; that is actually what is happening when the Bank of Canada buys up $75 million of these Treasury Bills. Instead of privately controlled financial institutions getting these profits, the people get them.
Well, Mr. Speaker, we will not continue talking about that. However, I should like to advance one proposal which I believe would be of great benefit to Canada. This proposal is not new. Members of this party have presented it before this House before, and my predecessor, Mr. Solon Low, referred to it during the bank legislation revision in 1954. We believe the Minister of Finance would be well advised to establish a permanent monetary commission composed of men who represent the Bank of Canada, the chartered banks, the Department of Finance and various aspects of our economy such as agriculture, labour, industry, and private business in general. Such a monetary commission might well be an extension of the board of the Bank of Canada, meeting regularly to consider all these matters related to financial and monetary policy of the Federal Government. This commission would not be silently responsible to some unseen power or authority, but would be able to answer directly to the representatives of the Canadian people sitting in the House of Commons. Likewise, they would be able to report through the Auditor General as the public accounts are reported today, making it possible to deal with financial and monetary matters before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
It would be a means also of keeping Members informed about the Government's monetary policy, thus keeping the public informed as well. An informed public makes for a strong democracy as well as a strong Parliament. I am convinced such a permanent monetary commission would provide the answer to many of the problems we face in our economy today, problems which I do not believe are being given sufficient attention in our thinking to provide the answers. We
June 14, IS65



would get from such a commission an independent report periodically. In this way the Members of this House would be able to keep their fingers much closer on what was actually happening in the functioning of our economic system. The commission could be charged with overseeing the policy drafted and set up by the House of Commons; and overseeing and managing could include a very important point, one which I think is of tremendous importance to the people of Canada, and that is the decennial revision of the Bank Act which we are debating now.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would say that what we need in Canada today is a desirable economy. A desirable economy might be expressed as an economy which utilizes all modern methods of production, but which at the same time offers equitable employment for all. I suggest that there is a national inventory level of purchaseable production which, when maintained by an effective demand, would bring about the desirable economy. "Effective demand" is when the people of Canada would have within their own hands the necessary purchasing power to buy those things which are necessary to enable the standard of living of which we are capable and which, at the same time, would solve the problem of distribution that presently faces us. Certainly, our problem today in the economy is not one of production nor one of consumption, so long as there are people in Canada or in the world who need the things we can produce. As long as there are people who need what we can produce, there can be no surplus. What we need is an effective demand that will move the production of which we are capable into the hands of those who produced it and who wish to consume it. This should be the function of a desirable economy.
It is through the effective functioning of our banking system, it is through the policies that are laid down in the legislation regarding banking by this House, that such a desirable economy can be brought about. I just emphasize, therefore, that the meetings of the committee to which this legislation is going to be referred, this whole question of bringing about the proper type of legislation to control monetary policy through our banking system, should deal with this important matter connected with the welfare of the country.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with interest to a portion of this debate. Unfortunately, I could
Bank Act
not be here all the time because of other duties in my office and elsewhere. I must say I have listened with great interest to the hon. Member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson). I can never quite understand our Social Credit friends, Mr. Speaker, because if they were to give effect to the ideas they put forward in this House concerning Social Credit, we would have a socialist democratic form of Government. There is no question about it. I cannot understand why they want to socialize credit without accepting the full social responsibility of such action.

May I ask the hon. Member a question? Does he not think it would be much better to consider socializing our credit to preserve and strengthen a private enterprise economy, than it would to turn it over to state ownership?

I am glad to answer that question. If we socialize our credit, then what we have actually done is to assume federal social responsibility over the economy, upon which could be based legitimate private enterprise which also recognized its responsibility to the community.
[DOT] (7:30 p.m.)
Mind you, Mr. Speaker, I realize these people have a germ of an idea in which there is a basis of truth. The only thing is that they will not come quite far enough along the road.
To the majority of people, banking has been a mystery every since the Rothschilds financed Wellington at the Battle of Waterloo, and Napoleon on the other side. Later they made a big profit as a result of a messenger going to Britain and informing the Rothschilds of the victory of Wellington, before the government knew.
And the people of Great Britain are still paying the interest on that.
That is quite right. The people of Great Britain are still paying interest on debts incurred during the Napoleonic wars, and later.
Would the hon. Member permit a question?
Certainly.

I am sure the hon. Member would not want his statement to reverberate down through history about Rothschild financing Wellington at Waterloo. Was it not a fact that he got advance notice of Wellington's victory at Waterloo, and as a result of that made a fortune?

June 14, 1965
Bank Act

They financed both governments in the Napoleonic wars, but the House of Rothschild was substantially founded on the profits made as a result of Wellington's victory at Waterloo. I think we are both correct. Anyway, this question has always been a mystery to the average man.
The late former Prime Minister, Mackenzie King, recognized this fact when he said something to this effect in the House, recognizing as he did the power over the economy that was in the hands of those who control credit- "Give me control of the credit of any nation and I will control that nation." I am sure our present Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) has the same point of view, only he has not expressed it so forcefully. However, there will come a time in the not too distant future when the Members of our party will have allies in the Members of the Social Credit party and the Creditistes in the cause of social control of credit, and at some later date, possibly 25 or 30 years hence, we can expect to get allies from the Progressive Conservative party.
I give the Minister credit for having an appreciation of the responsibility of the banks to the nation as a whole. I understand that this bill is to be referred to a committee- I have forgotten its exact name.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.

My hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) says it is Finance, Trade, Economic affairs and what not. Anyway, I trust this committee will take every opportunity not only to inform its members but all Members of the House and the people of this country on how the banking system works.
I just want to place on record some ideas that have been given to me by a person who believes we can improve the service rendered the nation by the banks by a combination of public control through legislation and private operation. I think my friends in the Social Credit group would go along with his ideas, and I just mention them because I have had considerable correspondence with this gentleman and think he should be called before the committee to explain his ideas; he gives a program for mobilization of money under federal control in a five year plan.
What is his name?

Richard H. Babbage. Possibly he is known to the Minister. Anyway, his general idea is, and I quote:

An extended banking system supervised by the Bank of Canada pursuant to existing statutes enacted by the Parliament of Canada.
Designed to consolidate:
1.	Federal control of currency and credit:
2.	Provincial control of natural resources;
3.	Effective financial supervision of all organizations operating in public ownership.
Then he goes on to deal with the organization of this type of plan, and first he says:
1.	Establish in the Bank of Canada a separate account for each provincial government.
2.	Set up a national revolving fund as a federal government account in the Bank of Canada made up as follows:-
(a)	Revenues of all government agencies. Departments, Crown Corporations and Canadian Wheat Board.
(b)	All chartered bank reserves and rest funds.
(c)	Special payments received by the Government of Canada.
(d)	Reserves of Life Insurance Companies.
(e)	Revenues of all public utility corporations.
(f)	Pension fund holdings of federal government bonds.
(g)	General public holdings of federal government bonds.
(h)	Branch line rationalization fund.
All the foregoing deposits would remain in chartered banks as agents for the Bank of Canada.
Then he goes on to suggest:
Deposit accounts enumerated above would be designated "Special Account (Control)" in Bank of Canada ledgers. Expenditures debited to such accounts would require federal Cabinet Order in Council. This procedure is followed by the Canadian Wheat Board at present.
The national revolving fund, holding currencies of countries trading with Canada, could finance all foreign aid programs. Similarly, obligations to the United Nations and NATO could be serviced, as well as interest on the national debt which could be liquidated progressively.
I hope my friends in the Social Credit group are following me.
Forming a continuous flow of flexible money supply the national revolting fund would finance all projects for the good of Canada in keeping with special powers allotted to the provinces in the B.N.A. Act subject to Cabinet authorization.
Credit demands by private individuals and corporations would be serviced and provided by chartered banks, solely, under free competition as to interest rates.
All government grants, subsidies, subventions and state insurance for private profit enterprise would cease. Risk capital, unhampered by taxation on consumption by Government at three levels, would have fair administration subject to the rule of law.
Any doubt about the capacity of Canadian chartered banks to furnish loans (both long and short-term) for greatly stimulated activity in farm and factory, is dispelled by statistics, published recently, in American Banker Magazine, which rates two Canadian banks among the ten largest banks in the free world, judged by size of deposits.
How Canadian banks stood in that list appears as follows:
Royal Bank of Canada (8)	$4,686,339,000
Canadian Imperial Commerce (9)	4,529,904,000
June 14, 1965

Bank of Montreal (17 )	3,709,920,000
Toronto Dominion (44)	2,109,450,000
Bank of Nova Scotia (47)	2,037,221,000
These five banks hold liquid assets of Canadian depositors aggregating $17,072,834,000. Assuming an average cash ration of 8 per cent, that amount of liquidity would finance loan demands in excess of $213,000,000,000.
I mention this because I have had a lot of correspondence with this gentleman who, I think, has something for us to consider in the ideas he has put forward.
The more rapid and radical changes induced in our way of life by science, the greater is the need for social stability made possible by organized sharing of potential hazards.
More than two-thirds of income tax, collected by the federal Government at present, comes out of pay envelopes of all who earn salaries and wages. This represents the most acutely felt "potential hazard" afflicting the Canadian population today. Financing through a national revolving fund would pull deduction slips from pay envelopes.
Mobilization of money operating under federal control in compliance of laws of Canada would, at once, ensure absolute control of the public purse by the House of Commons, notwithstanding anything in any part of the constitution.
This is a very interesting idea and does provide an opportunity for the federal social control of credit, and yet do it through the chartered banks. In my opinion, a person with such a policy should have an opportunity to appear before the committee, express his views, and be questioned. I simply rise to suggest that this committee has an opportunity, if the committee majority agree to accept that opportunity, to call persons and witnesses before it to gather their ideas not only with respect to our banking system as it is now, but to the system as it might be amended or altered. In so doing they would inform members of this House as to the way in which the banking system operates and how it could be improved. The population of Canada generally would also be provided with important information on this subject. Not only could we amend the Bank Act, but in so doing we could give the people generally an understanding of the way in which credit is distributed for the development of our economy. If this committee undertakes its responsibility not only to the Government and to the House but to the people of this country generally we would have some knowledge of the effect of bank policies upon our economic health and future development. [DOT] (7:40 p.m.)
That is all I have to say, now. I think these ideas, as well as the ideas which have been put forward by others, should be given consideration. Even the ideas of the hon.
Bank Act
Member for Red Deer (Mr Thompson), should be considered. If he wishes to go before the committee and outline in detail how the program put forward by his hon. friends would affect our economic development, I think he should be given the opportunity to do so.
