speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It has been suggested recently that
clause 75(2)(g) is restrictive and unfair in its application to the Mercantile Bank of Canada. There seems to be considerable misunderstanding about the facts of the matter, which are as follows:
The proposed bill includes sections which:
(a)	will ensure that control of the Canadian banks-apart from the Mercantile-will be retained in Canadian hands;
(b)	will restrict non-resident participation to 25 per cent of the shares of any bank;
(c)	will restrict the holdings of any single shareholder or group of shareholders-foreign or domestic-to 10 per cent of the shares;
(d)	will not permit Canadian banks to control other corporations including trust and loan companies.
The Government is anxious to see a number of new banks incorporated. Therefore, in the initial stages in order to encourage this, it is not proposed that the limitation of shareholdings to 10 per cent will apply. However, such new banks will be subject to the provisions of clause 75(2)(g) which will limit their total resources to 20 times their authorized capital until such time as their shares are more widely distributed, and no single person or group holds more than 10 per cent.
The Mercantile Bank of Canada is a wholly owned subsidiary of the International Banking Corporation which, in turn, is owned by the First National City Bank of New York. I understand that International Banking Corporation also owns all the shares of International Trust Company, which is a Canadian trust company operating in Canada.
All this places the First National City Bank of New York in a preferred position on three counts:
(i)	It owns all the shares of a Canadian bank, something that no one else will be permitted to do.
(ii)	It owns both a chartered bank and a trust company in Canada, something no other bank or anyone else will be permitted to do.

June 14, 1965
Bank Act
(iii)	It is the only foreign bank which may conduct a banking business in Canada.
In these circumstances, the question arises whether the provisions of clause 75(2)(g) which will apply in the case of all other banks in Canada, should be applicable to the Mercantile.
It is argued on behalf of Mercantile that the application of clause 75(2)(g) will be restrictive and therefore that it is unfair to the owners of that bank. I cannot accept this suggestion of unfairness. This whole matter was very fully discussed with representatives of the First National City Bank of New York before they acquired the shares of Mercantile.
On July 18, 1963, Mr. James Stillman Rockefeller, President of the First National City Bank of New York, and Mr. Robert McFadden, an officer of that bank and now President of the Mercantile Bank of Canada, called upon me in my office here in the Parliament Buildings. Mr. R. B. Bryce, Deputy Minister of Finance, and Mr. Clayton Elder-kin, Inspector-General of Banks, were present during the discussion.
Mr. Rockefeller informed me that his bank had made an arrangement with the shareholders of Mercantile to acquire the shares of the latter bank but that no firm commitment had been made with them. I interpreted this to mean-or at least I did to begin with- that no commitment would be made to buy the shares in question if the entry into Canada of the First National City Bank was not looked upon with favour by the Canadian Government. I said I was glad to have an opportunity of expressing the views of the Government in this matter because, while we were aware of the size, importance and standing of the First National City Bank of New York, there would be some objections to the proposed purchase.
I said I quite realized it would be legally possible in this way for the First National City Bank to acquire a banking subsidiary in Canada. This rather unique circumstance amounted in effect to a loophole in the law which requires that bank charters be approved by Parliament. Because of this, First National City Bank could establish a subsidiary here which might be expanded into a large foreign-owned banking institution- unless subsequent action were taken when the Bank Act came up for revision.
I pointed out that if the First National City Bank entered the Canadian banking field in this way, it was probable that other United States banking corporations would wish to do

so as well-but in that case either new charters would have to be obtained or such other United States banking corporations would have to purchase a controlling interest in one of the existing Canadian banks. I said the latter course would not be looked upon with favour by the Canadian Government and I added that it was highly unlikely that a new charter would be granted by this Parliament for a bank that was to be nonresident controlled. I said the Government would not be in favour of any such action.
I emphasized that the situation then, that is, in mid-1963, was different from what it had been in 1953 when the Mercantile received its charter. Since that time, the Royal Commission on Canada's Economic Prospects had recommended that control of Canadian chartered banks should be held by Canadians. I said that following receipt of the report of the Royal Commission on Banking and Finance the Government would have to decide how the Bank Act should be revised, and in particular what should be done to ensure that control of the Canadian banking system remains in Canadian hands.
I informed the representatives of the First National City Bank that normally it would be unfair to apply retroactively any legislative restrictions on control of banks by non-residents. However, I said that since the First National City Bank were now aware of the Government's views, and had not at this time purchased control of Mercantile, the Government would not consider they were entitled to any special exemption from legislation in respect of foreign ownership that might be brought down in the future.
After a very full discussion, I advised the representatives of the First National City Bank of New York not to proceed with their proposed action until after the Bank Act was revised. There was no misunderstanding on the part of any of those present as to exactly what was meant. The representatives of the First National City Bank of New York were given clear notice of the Government's views. They were forewarned about the kind of legislation that might be expected when the Bank Act came up for review. I pointed out that Mr. Rockefeller and Mr. McFadden had sought an interview with me to ascertain the views of the Canadian Government before proceeding with a certain transaction. They had now been informed of the Government's views in categorical terms.

Would the hon. gentleman permit one question?

It is difficult to understand why the representatives of the First National City Bank of New York would have sought an interview with me as Minister of Finance if they had planned to go ahead with the transaction regardless of the views of the Canadian Government. They did so with their eyes open.

Hear, hear.

speechtext: For some time I have been looking forward to the opportunity of replying to some of the arguments and opinions put forward by Social Credit Members relating to our banking system and our banking legislation.
What about those of the hon. Member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge)?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The revisions which we now propose making to the banking legislation do not represent any departure from the
Bank Act
principles on which our monetary system has been established, so they raise no new questions of this nature. However it is natural that hon. Members who feel strongly on these matters should wish to take this occasion to advance in detail some of the views they have expressed in the past, and which are founded on the belief that there are fundamental defects in our monetary and financial system which need to be remedied.
Let me say first of all that I believe the general understanding of economics up until about 30 years ago was inadequate for the task of analysing the working of the financial system. It was understandable, therefore, that various monetary reform movements, including Social Credit, should arise. In the past 30 years, however, great progress has been made in analysing the working of our economy, thanks very largely to the basic ideas developed by John Maynard Keynes, and since applied widely throughout the world.
As a consequence of the progress made in the last three decades, it is not necessary to be a Social Crediter these days to understand that the supply of money occupies an important place in our economy, or that its proper management is essential if we are to achieve our economic objectives. I mentioned these objectives, hon. Members may remember, in the third paragraph of the budget speech, which can be found on page 427 of Hansard.
Our economic objectives are essentially in terms of real things-real goods and services -and the way they are distributed among Canadians. The essential purpose of our monetary system is to enable the economic system, as a whole, to produce the goods and services Canadians want, and to distribute them.
If we are to secure a high and sustainable level of economic growth, the money supply must grow along with our other economic magnitudes. This is well recognized both by the Government and by the Bank of Canada. In this connection I might refer hon. Members to what I said in the Budget speech in regard to monetary policy and liquidity, and to what the Governor of the Bank said in his annual reports; for example, on the first page of the report for 1964. Our present monetary system is one which enables this growth in the money supply to be brought about fairly and sensibly under the careful day-to-day management of the Bank.
There is, I think, no question in any of our minds now of the necessity of this growth

June 14, 1965
Bank Act
in the money supply, or of the need to manage it, in order to achieve our economic objectives. The preamble to the Bank of Canada Act constitutes an early statement by Parliament a generation ago of the desirability to establish a bank to carry out this management of the money supply to promote the economic and financial welfare of the nation. Where we and most other people differ with the hon. Members who espouse Social Credit doctrines is in the causes for the necessity of the expansion in the money supply, in the means by which it should be brought about, and in the degree to which it should and can safely take place.
Social Credit theory, as I understand it, argues that there is an inherent deficiency in our economic system which leads always to an insufficiency of the supply of money. There have been, I know, a number of arguments of various degrees of sophistication as to what gives rise to this deficiency. These were fashionable a generation or so ago, and some hon. Members may recall them in connection with the "A plus B" theorem. I have never been convinced that there was such an inherent deficiency. I have been convinced, however, that management of the money supply was necessary both to enable the economy to reach its full potential at any particular time and also to enable it to achieve a high and sustainable rate of growth.
However, I do not believe there is any point in going into this theoretical question of inherent deficiencies at this time. What we need to ensure is that we have a monetary system which enables the money supply to be properly managed and to be expanded or restrained from time to time in the degree that is desirable in the public interest.
Our present monetary system does permit an effective, flexible control over the money supply to be achieved. This control is exercised by the Bank of Canada in varying the amount of cash in the banking system. The main method by which the Bank of Canada affects the amount of cash in the system is by buying and selling Government securities from and to the public. The sale of securities reduces the supply of cash, since purchasers of the securities pay for them by turning over cash in their bank accounts to the Bank of Canada. The purchase of securities by the Bank of Canada increases the supply of cash, since the Bank pays for those securities by handing over cheques drawn on itself which are then deposited mainly in the chartered banks.
The chartered banks must maintain minimum cash reserves with the Bank of Canada -8 per cent of their deposit liabilities under the present law, and 7 per cent under the law as now proposed. This requirement is, as it were, the first call on the increase in their deposits resulting from Bank of Canada purchases of securities from the public. When that requirement is met, the banks may increase their loans and buy securities themselves, up to the point where the resultant increase in the deposit liabilities requires a further increase in their minimum reserve deposits with the Bank of Canada.
It is thus the combination of open market operations by the Bank of Canada and the minimum reserve requirement which essentially determines the volume of deposits in the chartered banks. And it is the volume of deposit liabilities of the chartered banks which essentially determines the supply of money, the supply of bank credit, and indirectly, through the complicated market mechanism described in the report of the Royal Commission, the volume and terms of other credit in our financial markets. I might refer hon. Members, who have not had an opportunity of reading it, to chapter 6 of the Royal Commission's report which deals with this. The nature of the system permits a day-to-day control to be exercised and the effects of any adjustments to be noted and assessed when subsequent changes are under consideration.
[DOT] (8:00 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, Social Credit critics claim that the control of the money in the economy rests with the private banking system. Moreover, it is claimed that the private banks can increase the amount of money in the country at will, and without cost to themselves. These claims are entirely wrong. The control of the amount of money in the economy rests with the public monetary authorities, that is, the Bank of Canada and the Federal Government. I might mention in parenthesis that the proposed amendments to the Bank of Canada Act, relating to the powers of the Bank of Canada and the Federal Government, spell out in greater detail than hitherto exactly where the power does reside. The money supply can only be increased in so far as the Bank of Canada supplies the necessary cash which flows into the chartered banks and increases their deposits. The banks can only increase the money supply within the scope given them by the Bank of

June 14. 1965

Canada and they must maintain the confidence of the public in order to attract and retain deposits.
If the amount of cash in the system is increased the banks compete for their share of it. This they do by inducing individuals to deposit with them any additional cash they may have. These deposits represent a liability of the bank to the depositor on which interest may be paid by the bank to the depositor and in respect of which services must be rendered. If a bank's cash reserves are increased by the action of a depositor the bank is in a position to increase its earning assets by making loans or buying securities. Indeed, a bank must increase its earning assets if its deposits increase significantly, since deposits involve a cost to the bank. In the process of increasing its assets the banking system's total deposit liabilities will increase up to the point where its cash reserves, which are controlled by the Bank of Canada, are equal to the required cash ratio-or nearly so. The banking system's total deposit liabilities and its total assets cannot exceed the limit thus established. Any individual bank can increase its loans and investments only to the extent that it has attracted and can retain deposits. So that if for any reason an individual bank's depositors decide to reduce their balances with that bank it must to that extent draw on its assets, first by running down its cash and then by making good the loss of each through liquidating other assets in order to maintain the required cash ratio. The success of an individual bank depends on its ability to induce the public to hold its liabilities.
I turn now to the question of the degree of monetary expansion, which is the third source of our difference with Social Credit. While the difference here is of great importance, it may be fair to say it is one of emphasis and degree. Many exponents of Social Credit imply that large increases in the supply of money can safely be made, and indeed should be made, except perhaps at times when clearly the economy is at full employment and under strain. We believe, on the other hand, that the increase in the supply of money has to be carefully controlled and determined after careful economic analysis and the application of good judgment to appraisal of the economic situation. If the increase in the amount of money is too little, credit stringency may inhibit the desirable economic expansion of growth. But if, on the other hand, the increase in the money supply is too much, it will lead to
Bank Act
price and cost increases and to balance of payments difficulties. If such increases in the money supply and consequent increases in the pressure of expenditure in the economy should persist, we can expect that ultimately they will lead to inflation and, in a country such as ours, to an exchange crisis.
I do not believe that the proponents of Social Credit feel that price increases and inflation constitute a serious danger; indeed, in their view it is better to run these risks than to suffer a deficiency in expenditure for purposes either of employment or of social justice. In my view they greatly underrate the dangers inherent in such attitudes. This is the chief weakness in their approach to our financial problems.
Quite apart from the effects on the balance of payments and the exchange position, inflationary pressures are highly undesirable. In the first place, they produce an unstable situation which cannot last. They lead to speculation, to efforts to anticipate further price increases and to expenditures on many things both of a capital and current nature which are not justified by the long-run prospects of the economy. Moreover, these excesses are apt to be reversed in time when the public is unwilling any longer to accept the consequences of inflationary conditions and when the economic actions to which they have led have proven to be ill-founded.
Second, we must recognize that inflation is fundamentally unfair. It confers great benefits on the economically strong and sharp. Those who can quickly see what is going on, and can manoeuvre and bargain to take advantage of it will undoubtedly gain. They are not to be found only in one particular class in the community, but include many of those with strong economic bargaining power. They gain at the cost of the weak, the innocent and the uninformed. It is true that nowadays governments, under such circumstances, frequently come to the aid of the weak or the innocent. But there are always some whose plight is overlooked, who will not or cannot seek to protect themselves. It is these poeple who bear the burden of inflation. It is this unfairness in the distribution of benefits and costs which leads to the political and social trouble to which serious inflation almost inevitably brings nations, whether they be advanced industrial societies such as some in Europe after the First World War, or developing countries such as some in Latin America in more recent years.
The other chief danger arising from excessive expenditure associated with an ex-

June 14, 1965
Bank Act
cessive increase in the money supply is the effect on the balance of payments. Naturally, much of the excessive expenditure will create demands for imports as the limits of domestic production are approached or exceeded. These imports must be paid for by the use of foreign exchange from a nation's reserves or by borrowing abroad, or by setting in motion forces that will check other imports or increase exports. The solution of borrowing from abroad is not likely to be available if a country is clearly permitting excessive expansions in its money supply and expenditures to create the kind of situation I have discussed. The use of reserves can only go on for a limited period as nations cannot normally afford to hold sufficient reserves to finance a lengthy spree.
Consequently, the likely result of a prolonged period of excessive expenditure is apt to be a depreciation of the currency involved. We have before us the example of the United Kingdom now having to take stern action to meet the situation created by a moderate excess of expenditure in an economy operating at full stretch. Our own history affords two examples since the end of the war, arising out of different causes, of the necessity to meet serious shortages of foreign exchange by unpleasant emergency action.
When a country gets into balance of payments difficulties as a result of excessive expenditure, it is apt to find itself confronted by a crisis arising from the anticipation of further difficulties. The expectation that it will be forced to permit its currency to depreciate naturally leads people to take whatever action they can to protect themselves, either by delaying the acquisition of that [DOT]country's currency or expediting its sale, in carrying on commercial transactions. Moreover, both the residents of the country and others outside it who have invested in it are likely for reasons of ordinary prudence to want to protect themselves by moving their capital out of that country to somewhere else. It is this which gives rise to the need for vast sums to meet these capital movements under conditions where currencies appear threatened. This in turn calls for demonstrably effective measures to ensure that the excessive expenditures are being checked, unless of course the nation is prepared to see its exchange rate forced to a lower level.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
If by any chance it should ever appear that a Canadian Government was going to

apply Social Credit policies in a wholehearted way, I believe we could expect Canadians and others with investments here to move their capital out of Canada. I say this because those favouring Social Credit principles have given great emphasis to the increases in the money supply to which their doctrines lead. They have stressed the size of the programs they feel can be achieved by the application of these doctrines. Almost certainly this would undermine confidence in the currency on the part of all those who were in a position to protect themselves. In other words, as I have said before, any prospect of Social Credit theories being applied in practice would lead to a financial crisis in which the little fellow would be bound to suffer.
I should like to turn now to a number of specific points that have been brought forward by hon. Members favouring the Social Credit doctrine.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
First of all, I should like to comment on the implications of the proposal that banks should be required to hold 100 per cent cash reserves. Let me describe as briefly as I can the kind of situation which could be expected to prevail if the banks were required to match their deposit liabilities with assets held only in the form of cash, which earns nothing. That is what is meant when people suggest that the banks should be required to keep 100 per cent cash reserves against all deposit liabilities instead of holding, as at present, 8 per cent in the form of cash and 92 per cent in the form of interest bearing assets.
In these circumstances no bank could make a loan to a customer except from the relatively small amount of its own capital. It could not use savings deposited with it to finance business stock in trade, for example, or to buy seed grain. It could not assist a municipality to operate efficiently through the year when its tax receipts come in irregularly. It could not assist the private citizen to budget his major expenditures by providing funds when
June 14, 1S65

they are needed so that he can pay for the "big ticket" items over a period of time out of his current income. Because the bank would not be earning interest by making loans, it would not be able to provide the other services which people look for, except at greatly increased cost to the customer. The cost of paying a bill by cheque, for example, could increase to many times the present bank charge for handling a cheque.
Then, too, the citizen who placed his savings in the bank would quickly find that he was losing money. If the bank could not use deposits to make loans, it could not make interest payments to its depositors. Instead, it would have to charge customers with the full cost of safekeeping and maintaining accounts. The bank would be required to lend the savings of Canadians which had been deposited with it to the Bank of Canada without interest, to be lent in turn without interest to the Government for its purposes. Whether these purposes were good or bad, the arrangement would not be a fair deal for those who deposited their funds in the banks.
This is the essence of the proposed 100 per cent reserve system. It is a way for the Government to get the use of people's savings, their capital, deposited in banks without paying them interest on it. I do not believe that such a system could work to the advantage of the people of Canada. Moreover, if it ever should be tried in practice, people would keep only the barest minimum on deposit with the banks and invest their money in other institutions or in securities.
I should now like to comment as briefly as I can on the subject of interest on the public debt and whether it does indeed represent a burden or a loss of purchasing power, as some hon. Members have suggested. It is true that interest payments are an expenditure by Government. They must be provided for in the budget and we raise money by taxation to meet these costs. But almost all of Canada's national debt is held by Canadians. The interest payments made by the Government are a form of income in the hands of those Canadians who receive them. Government bonds provide a secure means of investment for the savings of the people, either directly in the form of Canada Savings Bonds or other Government obligations or indirectly through savings in pension funds, insurance companies, trust companies and similar institutions which invest substantial amounts in Government bonds. Thus the country as a whole does not lose
Bank Act
purchasing power as a result of the interest paid on the debt. A writing down of this debt or arbitrary reduction of interest payments would represent a loss of savings and of income to those who have saved for their old age or for emergencies. It would represent a loss, for example, to people who have protected themselves and their families through life insurance policies.
I had hoped the exposition of the working of the present monetary system given by the Royal Commission would have lifted the level of the debate on monetary theory to a discussion of modern issues based on a better understanding of the system. It is now generally accepted by those who understand the working of our economy that our monetary system must be well managed, and that is the case today. To try to convert our banking system to a 100 per cent cash reserve system, to try to create money to be lent to governments without interest, would be an irresponsible interference with the rights of millions of Canadians who save their money and keep part of it on deposit with our banks.
Canada is fortunate to have a good banking system that uses the savings deposited with it to help other Canadians to produce and sell what we need, or to finance purchases for later repayment. We can improve it in detail as we are now proposing to do. But we must not be deluded into thinking that all bank deposits can or should be diverted to Government purposes without interest. That would not only be grossly unfair to depositors but would destroy the essential role which the banks play in financing primary producers, consumers and businesses of all kinds.
As I said a minute ago, I have made these remarks because I promised, and have been promising to do so, and this seemed to me a good opportunity. I felt that hon. Members of the Social Credit parties had spoken not infrequently on this general subject and that they were entitled to a careful reply, which is what I have tried to give them this evening. In conclusion I should like to urge my friends in the two Social Credit parties to abandon theories that are obsolete and are based on clearly demonstrated misconceptions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There are two main points I should like to cover in opening the debate on the resolution to amend the Income Tax Act. First I should like to deal with the cut in personal income taxes which is to become effective on July 1. Then I should like to discuss briefly the proposal dealing with periodicals and newspapers.
Perhaps the most important section of this resolution deals with the tax cut to become effective on July 1, 1965. Understandably, this has been very well received by the public. Also understandably, there have been 22620-152
Income Tax Act
those who have suggested the cut might have taken some other form. I should like to say something about this.
As I explained in the budget speech, the total amount of the cut took into account the economic consequences resulting from the change and also the condition of the Budget. I pointed out that there is no precise mathematical formula that can be applied-it is a matter of judgment. It is our judgment that taking all considerations into account, we should plan for a tax cut of $250 to $275 million for a full year and that this should begin half way through this calendar year, which will be on July 1.
Having decided upon the amount of the cut, we then had to decide where it should be applied. I would like to quote what I said about this in the budget speech as reported at page 440 of Hansard.
In choosing the nature and form of the reduction, I have been influenced by the fact that we are expecting to make a thorough revision of our tax structure after receiving the report of the Royal Commission on Taxation and discussing the whole situation with the provinces. While we can count on none of our taxes being unaffected by such a revision, I have concluded that we should leave both the sales tax and the corporation income tax largely as they are pending this review.
In other words, we decided to apply the full amount of the cut to personal income taxes.
The Presidents of the Canadian Manufacturers Association and the Canadian Chamber of Commerce have expressed the view that cuts should have been made in corporation income taxes. However, neither of these gentlemen has indicated how in his opinion such a cut in corporation income taxes should be applied. The present rate of Federal tax after the abatement to take account of Provincial tax, is 12 per cent on the first $35,000 of taxable income, and 41 per cent on everything above that amount. The rate on the first $35,000 is a relatively low one by any comparative standard, even when the 9 per cent abatement for the provinces is included.
It is not clear if business spokesmen who have advocated immediate reduction of corporation income taxes have in mind a cut both in the rate on the first $35,000 of income, or only in the top rate of tax. We expect the Carter Commission will have a lot to say about the corporation income tax. And quite frankly, the Government did not wish to prejudge the case by taking action in advance of their report.
Moreover, it is well known that corporation profits, both before and after taxes, are

running at an all-time high. Corporation cash flows are also at an all-time high, thanks in large measure to the very generous provision for capital cost allowances provided for in the 1963 budget and extended in this recent budget. I mention these facts because they also have a bearing upon decisions in this field.
Some of those who favour a reduction in personal income taxes felt it should have taken another form. Mr. Gordon Sinclair, a well known broadcaster and an old friend of mine-he and I think we are about the only two people left who were not only born in Toronto but who have lived there ever since -advocated increasing the basic exemption to $2,000 for a single person and to $4,000 for married persons. The effect of this would have been to reduce federal and provincial revenues together, not by $250 million to $270 million but by $1,700 million. All I can say is that to have done this would have been highly irresponsible. I wrote to Mr. Gordon Sinclair about this and he was kind enough to read my letter over the air. I find that he has a very wide audience, judging from the comments that I received. He also wrote back and said that was fine, that I was entitled to my opinion but he was inclined to go at these things emotionally rather than statistically. That is his privilege, but I am not in that happy position when it comes to tax cuts.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
I might point out that the present exemptions in Canada are considerably higher than those in either the United States or the United Kingdom. In the United States the basic exemption plus standard deductions for single persons is $200 less than it is in Canada, and for married persons it is $500 less. In the United Kingdom the basic exemption is $225 less than it is here for single persons, and $740 less for married persons. I put these figures on the record because I think some people have felt that the exemptions in Canada were less generous than in other countries, and this just is not the case.
The New Democratic Party proposed that personal income tax exemptions be raised by $500 for single persons and $1,000 for married persons, and in addition that the old age security payment should be increased to $100 a month.

Mr. Chairman, could I ask the Minister if he has read the amendment that I pre-

sented to the House, because I did not make any such proposal.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The fact is that the form in which the proposed reduction in personal income tax is to be made was chosen for a number of reasons. We wanted to ensure that the reduction would confer the same benefit on people with similar incomes no matter where they resided in Canada, and that it would not disrupt the financial plans of the Provinces. This led us to the conclusion that the reduction should be in the form of a flat percentage of what is known as basic tax, rather than in the form of an increase in exemptions or a change in the rate schedule.
At present all the provinces impose a personal income tax, and in all provinces except Quebec the provincial tax is a percentage of the federal basic tax. Thus a decrease in the federal basic tax resulting from an increase in exemptions or a change in the rate schedule would have automatically reduced the amount of the provincial personal income taxes in all provinces except Quebec. It would also have automatically reduced the abatement allowed from the federal basic tax on acount of provincial tax. Because of this, a tax reduction of say $100 for a resident of a typical province other than Quebec would have turned out to be a federal tax cut of $76 and a provincial tax cut of $24. For a resident of Quebec, for whom the abatement would be larger under the opting-out arrangements, an intended reduction of $100 would have turned out to be a federal tax cut of only $53. There would have been no provincial tax cut, since the Province of Quebec levies its tax without reference to the federal tax.
It follows that a tax reduction in these forms-that is, an increase in the exemptions or a change in the rates-would have resulted in different amounts of reductions for taxpayers residing in different provinces but whose circumstances were otherwise the same. It would also have seriously disrupted the financial plans of the provinces.
Of course the nine provinces could, in such circumstances, have raised their rates to avoid a decrease in their personal income tax revenues, but this would have been difficult for them and especially difficult for those provinces that had introduced their budgets before the Federal Budget was 22620-152J
Income Tax Act
presented. Similarly, the Province of Quebec could, at the cost of a considerable reduction in its revenues, have lowered its rates so that the income tax position of a resident of Quebec, taking both federal and provincial personal income taxes into acount, was the same as that of a resident of other provinces. We did not believe that federal action that would have necessitated such changes in every province could be justified when the method chosen was available to us. Under it, the whole of the tax reduction will be borne by the Federal Government, and under it the benefits to taxpayers all across Canada will be the same. I wanted this opportunity, Mr. Chairman, to make that explanation, especially to those who have had some misunderstanding as to the reason we proposed the cut in this way.
The second point that I would like to discuss at this stage is the section of the resolution which deals with periodicals and newspapers. I would like to review briefly the events which have led up to the measures which are designed to engure that control of our periodicals and newspapers will be retained in the hands of Canadians. Hon. Members will recall that a Royal Commission was created by the previous Government to examine the position of Canadian periodicals. This was the O'Leary Commission, whose chairman is a respected Canadian editor known for his strong views on many subjects including, as one would expect, fiercely held convictions about the vital importance of maintaining freedom of the press.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
The Commission, which reported in 1961, stressed the importance to the country of Canadian self-expression through Canadian ownership and control of periodicals. It recommended as a practical way of securing such control that those directing advertising to Canadian readers should use Canadian publications as a condition of the costs being recognized as a business expense for tax purposes.
The previous Government accepted this recommendation, though with the qualification that it should not apply to foreign owned periodicals already published in Canada; that is, to Time and Reader's Digest. That Government fell, however, before these proposals were approved by Parliament.
This Government, after giving the matter further consideration, decided that the measure proposed by our predecessors was a sound

June 14. 1965
Income Tax Act
one. This decision was announced in the Throne Speech of February, 1964. My recollection is that while the announcement in February, 1964, and the earlier announcement by the previous Government aroused some controversy, most of such controversy was centred on the exemption provided for Time and Reader's Digest. The principle of disallowing advertising costs as deductions for tax purposes was not challenged, as I remember, in the press or elsewhere.
In explaining the proposal in the House on February 20, 1964, the Prime Minister pointed out that the problem of Canadian ownership of periodicals applied also to other media of communications. In particular, he mentioned "signs that metropolitan newspapers in Canada may, before long, be in danger of coming under foreign ownership and control". The Prime Minister stated that the Government would give careful consideration to this problem.
Hon. Members will remember that the 1964 session was an extended one-to put it mildly-and we did not have time to deal with the resolution on periodicals. In the meantime, further consideration was given to the broader problem, especially to the question of ownership and control of Canadian newspapers. This included informal discussions with a number of newspaper publishers.
As a result of this further consideration and discussion, it was decided that the same principle which had been recommended by the Royal Commission and put forward first by the previous Government and then by this Government in the February, 1964, Throne Speech, should be applied to newspapers as well as periodicals.
As I said, this had not aroused opposition or suggestions that it posed a threat to the freedom of the press when it was to be applied to periodicals. It has been surprising, therefore, that this charge should be raised when the same principle is now to be applied to newspapers. It is difficult to accept the fact that a principle can be right and good, and widely accepted as such, when applied to one field of communications but not When it is applied to another.
The Government's proposal asserts no control whatever over newspapers or other publications. It does not alter in any way the complete freedom of businesses to advertise in any way they choose in existing publications or in any future publications owned by Canadians. It provides no precedent for any

kind of Government interference in the complete freedom of the press.
The proposal does make it highly unlikely, however, that the ownership of Canadian newspapers will be transferred to foreigners. Some few people may not think it matters whether control of Canadian communications media is retained in Canadian hands. The Government believes this does matter, and the majority of newspaper publishers have indicated that they share this view.
Hon. Members will recall that in the early days of radio, following the report of the Aird Commission, approval was given to legislation providing that control of Canadian radio stations-and later television stations- must be held by Canadians. If this had not been done, it is safe to assert that many Canadian radio and television stations would now be controlled by absentee owners.
There are, of course, similar laws in the United States respecting the ownership of U.S. television and radio stations, as an exCanadian, Mr. Jack Kent Cooke discovered.
As I say, the majority of newspaper publishers have not objected to preventive measures being taken against the transfer of Canadian newspapers to non-residents. The controversy seems to arise over the timing and the method chosen to prevent this being done.
As to the timing, let me say the obvious. There is no point in locking the stable door after the horse has been stolen. Hon. Members will recall that last September I announced that legislation would be proposed in due course preventing the acquisition of any of our chartered banks by non-residents of Canada, and that this would be made retroactive to the time of the announcement; that was, to September, 1964. I was asked why it was necessary to make an announcement at that time when, as far as most people knew, no takeovers of Canadian banks were in contemplation. Shortly after making the announcement, however, I discovered that a foreign institution had planned to acquire a controlling interest in one of our principal Canadian banks. We would have been faced with a fait accompli if it had not been for my announcement.
The same thing could be true in the case of some Canadian newspapers. I do not think we would like it very much if we woke up one morning to find, for example, that control of the Toronto Globe and Mail had been acquired by certain United States interests who wished to exert a direct influence on
June 14. 1965

Canadian public policy. Nor do I think we would like it very much if we woke up one morning to find, for example, that control of La Presse had been acquired by certain European interests who wished to exert a direct influence on Canadian public policy. These are eventualities the Government believes we should guard against in time.
In essence, the objections boil down to the particular measure which is proposed to accomplish an objective with which most people agree. The fact is that no practical alternative has been found, despite careful thought and much discussion with the people concerned. In practical terms, we have the alternative of proceeding with the measure which is before the House or of dropping the question altogether. If we were to do the latter, and one or more of our more important newspapers or chains of newspapers were to fall into foreign hands, neither the Government nor Parliament could shirk responsibility for having allowed this to happen.
Let me say another word about the freedom of the press, or to put it in broader terms, the freedom of the communications media. First, measures which have prevented control of Canadian radio and television stations being acquired by non-residents have been generally accepted. Second, the present proposal with respect to Canadian periodicals has not been challenged, Third, clearly there is not and could not be any question of interfering with the press in so far as the dissemination of news and opinion is concerned. Fourth, the proposal interferes with one freedom and one freedom only. It means that a Canadian publisher wanting to sell his newspaper will have to accept the best bid he can get from other Canadians. The whole point is to establish a safeguard to prevent foreigners from outbidding Canadians in this field.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
I can understand the objections of publishers who may wish to expand their operations to other countries. Obviously, if this same approach were adopted elsewhere, such expansion would not be possible unless the parties concerned were prepared to apply for citizenship in such other countries as was done by Mr. Jack Kent Cooke. But this is an objection which should be stated clearly for what it is: fear that businessmen or wealthy financiers may be discouraged from acquiring the communications media of other countries and, having done so, perhaps attempting to influence public opinion in those
Income Tax Act
countries. That kind of objection should not be confused with freedom of the press.
Quite right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do believe, Mr. Speaker, that the discussion which has arisen over this issue has had its uses. The very proper concern of the press about its freedom has been vigorously stated. I cannot believe that after this discussion any Canadian Government at any time would ever contemplate any measure which could seriously be construed as interfering with the freedom of the press. I know that no Liberal Government would ever think of doing so. I am sure the same would be true of any Government composed of any of the other parties represented in this House.

Mr. Chairman, in dealing with this resolution we are faced with quite a compendium of bits and pieces having to do with various sections of the Income Tax Act. Some of them are as usual hole plug-gers, or perhaps it might be better to say "pluggers of holes". Then there is the particular section dealing with newspapers and periodicals on which the Minister has spoken for the last several minutes. It is not my intention tonight to deal with that latter aspect but rather with some of the other features of the resolution.
First of all, with regard to the income tax reduction I think personally that one is not being overly cynical if he says that this was devised and timed as part of a voting gimmick. Let me say why it seems to be a voting gimmick. When "10 per cent" is said quickly it sounds like a lot to people who are taxpayers, but it means nothing to nontaxpayers. It does not do anything for people not classed as taxpayers.
There have been other tax reductions in the past. In 1957 or 1958 the Minister's pred-esessor but one brought in a tax reduction which greatly increased the number of nonincome taxpayers. I think that what happened was that the Minister had about $250 million to $275 million to play with and he said to himself, "How am I going to put that to the best use politically"?
Huh.

It was straightforward political thinking. First of all, we know there were limitations in the case of some of the provinces, so far as the basic tax is concerned. I put it to the Minister and to the House that the tax proposal is discriminatory in a number of ways. First of all, as I said

June 14, 1965
Income Tax Act
it does nothing for the non-taxpayer of whom there are many in this country either by reason of limited income or because they have varying exemptions. I do not think the Minister of Fisheries will shake his head when by reason of exemptions a person becomes a non-taxpayer, and there are thousands in this category. Either by reason of the number of dependants or otherwise potential taxpayers become non-taxpayers. In other words, they are cleared by their exemptions. Ten per cent of nothing means nothing to such a person so he gets no gain.
For the person who pays a small amount of tax a 10 per cent reduction is a very minute amount. I am not going to go into the varying scales. These were adumbrated by my late colleague, the former Member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings, and also by others. References have been made to a cup of coffee a day and so on. But then there is a further category, and this is perhaps the main reason I consider this reduction political. Perhaps the hon. Member for Northumberland may not have thought about this.
I am thinking of those people whose incomes are above the level of incomes that will benefit from this reduction. In other words, on the average the limitation of $600 means that anyone with an income above $20,000 will not benefit. Some people will say that $20,000 is a lot of money and anyone with such an income is in the higher brackets in this country. But I put it to hon. Members that in so far as economic development and commercial impact are concerned taxpayers in this category are very important, because in the main most of those who earn over $20,000 are people who are perhaps a little more industrious.
A little luckier.
Less than 1 per cent of the population.
They are, shall we say, more energetic. Somebody says "a little luckier". I do not know that there are many people who are prepared to work 16 or 18 hours a day, who have considerable ingenuity-
The right father.

-and have not inherited wealth but have been very industrious people. They are not limited to any part of the country and they are somewhat restricted in number. I am sure that the official thinking goes this way: There are a certain number of these people who are dyed in the wool Lib-

erals, so no matter what we do they will still vote Liberal.
Hear, hear.

I have said there is a proportion. Then an equal number are Conservative and this action will only reinforce them in voting Conservative. But the overall number is not large. Then there is a third segment comprised of people who may have voted Liberal but will now vote against the Liberals because of this action. However, politically speaking, their number is small. I am sure the political thinking is: What is their political impact in votes? An analysis shows that in numbers right across the country throughout the constituencies their impact is not very great.
How many are there between $10,000 and $20,000?

There are more between $10,000 and $20,000 than there are over $20,000. But I would suggest this is an area of discrimination. It is not the only one, but it is an area of discrimination just as one might say that a progressive income tax is discriminatory. In other words, you just grin and bear it because you can bear it a little better if you are in a higher income bracket, even though your contribution is quite as much and in fact may be considerably more than the person whose income is somewhat less. The Minister indicated that it was not possible to do anything about corporation income tax, of which the Federal share is 12 per cent of incomes under $35,000 and 41 per cent on incomes above $35,000, because the provinces have a 9 per cent vested interest in corporation income taxes. He preferred to wait for the report of the tax structure committee.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
Well, I do not care how you slice a loaf of bread, lengthways or crossways, it still comes out bread. I think the Minister would agree with me, as would the hon. member for Northumberland, that the majority of corporate income tax is passed on to the consumer. It is still John Q. Citizen who pays the tax. Now, as to whether that tax cut should be an incentive or not, I subscribe to the view that corporate income tax would have much more impact than personal income tax, in so far as stimulation of the economy is concerned. After all, if I may say so, part of the political thinking behind this tax cut was to partially soften the impact of the premium that will be paid under the Canada
June 14. 1965

Pension Plan. The Minister was quite frank about this. There will be up to $79, and perhaps $158.40 payable by the self-employed person, under the Canada Pension Plan starting in 1966. This provision will, therefore, go toward softening the impact of this compulsory levy under the Canada Pension Plan.
I am just wondering if there would not have been more effect, in dealing with the $250 million or $275 million-the Minister's advisers may be able to help us in this regard -if there is that much available as a result of the growth of the gross national product, if we were to straighten up our corporate income tax structure and get away from this wholly artificial division between small business and big business, under which you get this 21 per cent and 50 per cent differentiation. I think it is wholly artificial.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Would my hon. friend permit a question?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is he recommending that this change should be made, that there should be this evening up? If so, does he think it should be done now or does he think we should wait for the Carter Commission report?

I am asking the Minister to see whether, within this field, there is not an area in which to work. After all, if we look at the motivation for the stimulation of the economy through a tax cut, we find it would do the most good in the field of corporate income tax. Is the Minister reinforcing my contention that this had a great deal of political gimmickry-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I thought I was asking the question, Mr. Chairman.
All right, I am coming back to it. I will answer by asking a question.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is the trouble with you lawyers.

If there is this $250 million or $275 million, I would have felt that an evening up of the two categories, with greater earnings withdrawn from a corporation in the shape of dividends, as is done in other jurisdictions, might help solve the problem of what I believe is an artificial distinction and would leave money-if the Minister will kindly bide with me-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You intrigue me.

This is not the first time I have made this suggestion. I made it last year,
Income Tax Act
the year before, and the year before that. As a matter of fact, my colleagues used to wonder if I was ever going to get off it. No one has as yet satisfactorily answered this point. It seems to me fundamentally unsound to set at $35,000-it used to be $25,000 and earlier it was $20,000-the distinction between small businesses and what is not really big business, especially if you go just $5,000 over the $35,000.
After all the Minister and his colleague, the Minister of National Revenue, from the experience I had with the Department of National Revenue, went through the greatest torture to plug up holes in the administration of the Income Tax Act, in so far as related companies were concerned. Certain types of industries and certain types of operations lend themselves to proliferation of departments or small companies. For some time certain corporate taxpayers were really in clover because they were able to break down their operations into a whole series of small businesses. Then we came along, again with an artificial restriction, and attempted to eliminate the related companies. Every year, as a result of the ingenuity of the taxpayers, the tax officials must come along and try to plug other holes. In my opinion the administration of the Income Tax Act in this particular sector would be a great deal easier and we would not have the expense on the part of the taxpayer trying to devise ways and means of alleviating the tax load-certainly at 50 per cent the tax load is heavy on corporations- if my suggestion were followed. I may be ahead of the Carter Commission, but I still believe that if there were $250 million or $275 million available for the full 1964-65 taxation year, something could have been done in the field of corporate income tax which, from the point of view of stimulating and maintaining the growth of our economy, would have been preferable to a personal income tax cut.
Then, we come down to the next paragraph of the income tax resolution and we see changes made which make allowances for the support of nephews and nieces, not all nephews and nieces, but those who may be infirm in certain categories either mentally or physically or, if they are over 21 years of age and attending a full time course of study at school or university, provided the mother of the niece or nephew is divorced or separated and is not in receipt of alimony or a similar payment.

June 14, 19G5
Income Tax Act
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
This may introduce a complication. If a separated mother receives alimony, and separate maintenance for her child, is it a lump sum? There is imprecision in the Act, and there is also the question if the father of the niece or nephew is deceased, or mentally or physically infirm.
This deals with a certain number of hardship cases, and I think generally Members will accept that there are always some of these fringe cases to which one feels one should be able to give relief, providing they do not cost too much money to the treasury. I can think of other categories which are equally deserving, but the numbers in them are too great and therefore they would be too costly to the treasury.
The fourth paragraph of the resolution deals with the famous amendment in the second half of the Canada Pension Plan, where a change was made in the old age security to those persons between 65 and 70 over the period until 1970, and the disallowance, as one became eligible for old age security, of the $500 allowance for being over age 65.
I must confess that on one occasion when I was commenting on this I said the Government was only giving something with the right hand and taking something back with the left hand, that the $500 not only covered the taxpayer but his or her spouse. I must confess I was temporarily in error and misled some people, and I must apologize for that. In any event this is part of phase 2 of the fourth version of the Canada Pension Plan, granting the old age security to persons over age 65.
So far as the fifth paragraph is concerned, this gives an extension of membership dues in either trade unions or professional societies, putting them outside of the $100 general allowance. In other words, full credit is being given for them.
Paragraph 6 deals with residence qualifications for persons in international service engaged in the development assistance programs of the Government of Canada. I dare say this is some inducement for persons engaging in this type of activity and it may also cover the Company of Young Canadians and people in it who may go abroad in the future.
So far as the seventh paragraph is concerned I would like to get a clarification from the Minister that any contributions made toward the Canada Pension Plan, or under

a provincial pension plan, may be deducted in computing the income of the persons making them. Is this within the limitations of any pension plan contributions, such as the $1,500 ceiling? We need some clarification on this point so that we may tell our constituents whether the introduction of the Canada Pension Plan will now be caught by the ceiling on retirement savings plans. There is a limitation within the framework of the Income Tax Act with regard to these contractual obligations that a taxpayer may enter into. Is this contribution to the Canada Pension Plan going to be in addition to that? The Minister nods his head, so I will take that as his answer.
In paragraph 10 there are a number of, shall we say, exemptions of expenses that heretofore have always proven somewhat thorny. I do not know why they have been brought in this year, as there are any number of others that are quite as difficult to handle, and it would be interesting to get a rationale from the Minister for the picking out of the five subparagraphs in paragraph 10 of the resolution.
The first one that comes to my mind is that if a payment is made by a taxpayer to a person who is a lessee of a property to induce that person to cancel the lease, then the taxpayer may claim that amount as a deduction or as an expense against that year's income, provided of course the lessee and the taxpayer are dealing at arm's length.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Which number?

Number 10 (a) on page 12 of the resolution. The first question that comes to my mind is why "dealing at arm's length"? Is this going to eliminate related companies? Is it also going to eliminate any personal relationship between the owner of the property, the taxpayer, and the lessee?
One example was quoted to me this way. A father has a shopping centre. One unit of the shopping centre he has leased to a son who is in independent business, and the other units are leased to strangers. The father is able to sell the shopping plaza, provided he is able to give vacancy. In other words, he must buy out the leases. The money that he has paid to the strangers he is able to claim as a deduction but the money he has paid to his son, who is in business independently, he cannot claim as a business expense, and to that extent I would say that this provision of dealing at arm's length is discriminatory and unrealistic, in the same way that I think there will be some difficulty in determining
June 14, 1965

the corporate relationships. What will be the criteria to determine whether two companies are at arm's length?
Also, what of the taxpayer who is a lessee and he buys off the term of his lease by a lump sum payment to his lessor? Is he not able to claim that? Surely to goodness the two positions should be treated the same way? For example, say I am renting premises under a long term lease and I have three years left, and because of expanding business conditions -I am sure the Minister would appreciate this-I feel I have got to go to bigger and better premises. Suppose I wish to buy out the balance of the term of the lease under which I hold the first premises, and I enter into an agreement with my landlord whereby in return for a lump sum payment I can bring the leasing agreement to a term. Certainly I should be able to claim that as a business expense. But I cannot do so under this provision.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
There is a second paragraph dealing with landscaping property used by the taxpayer for the purpose of gaining or producing income. If I landscape a house in which I live I cannot get any allowance under this provision. But if I own the house across the street I can claim the landscaping as an expense.
And move in yourself, the following year.

And, of course, as the hon. Member for Acadia says, I can move in myself the following year.
Then a deduction may be claimed in respect of clearing land or laying tile drainage for the purpose of carrying on a farm business. I think there is a good deal which could be done, here. It all depends, of course, on what the interpretation of "clearing land" is to be. Paragraph (d) is one which may lead us into a wilderness. It says-
-as or on account of the cost of making representations to a Government, municipality or other public authority in connection with a business carried on by the taxpayer, including representations for the purpose of obtaining a licence, permit, franchise or trademark.
What limitations are there to be? Is there to be an element of reasonableness? If there is, here is another point at which discretion is introduced on the part of the Minister. Will a taxpayer be able to bring forward all his expenses incurred in connection with, say, making representations to the Government of Canada for the purpose of obtaining a licence or a permit even if his efforts are 22620-153
Income Tax Act
unsuccessful and the proposed business cannot function? Take the case of a group of businessmen who get together to form a broadcasting company and apply for a television licence. They may spend a good deal of money toward obtaining a television licence and in the end they may not be successful. The expenses would be those of the corporate body which, in many instances, would have no income. To whom would the allowance be granted in such a case? Would it be set against the personal incomes of the individuals in the company? I think we shall need to obtain clear answers on points such as these, because there is a great deal of uncertainty attached to the resolution as presently written. As to expenses, does it mean a man would have to stay at a second rate or third rate hotel-or could he go down to the Chateau in Ottawa and live there like a visiting potentate? Is the Minister going to say expenses must be reasonable and, if so, who is to determine what is reasonable? Is this, too, to be left to ministerial discretion? These are questions which must be asked.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I must interrupt the hon. Member to remind him that the time allotted to him has expired.
Does the committee give leave to the hon. gentleman to continue?
Ten minutes.

I will not take that long.
Then I think we shall need some clarification of paragraph (e)-
-as or on account of the cost incurred in investigating the suitability of a site for a building or other structure planned by the taxpayer for use in connection with a business carried on by him.
Would this permit a man operating a business in Vancouver to travel to Montreal, all his expenses being deductible. Suppose the man says: I was investigating a site for a building which I may use; I am thinking of branching out. I trust these are questions to which the Minister will give us concise answers.
As I said earlier, I do not wish to deal with this matter of newspapers and periodicals except to say this: With regard to the periodicals, we heard a great deal of complaint from the Canadian periodical press that they were being starved to death because of what they alleged was unfair competition by two United States giants which had established operations in Canada, and which for technical reasons were able to acquire their editorial content at a much lower price than Canadian concerns. These two giants, it was

June 14, 1965
Income Tax Act
said, were syphoning off the great bulk of the advertising revenue available to magazines and other periodicals in Canada.
Well, the proposals contained in this resolution will only enshrine this situation because the two magazines in question, Time and Reader's Digest are specifically exempted. This resolution puts down in black and white the situation which has existed for a considerable time. From time to time the periodical press has activated discussion on this subject; at other times it has laid low. What is the future of Canadian magazines? Either they have been able to extricate themselves from this situation which existed prior to the appointment of the Royal Commission on press and periodicals, or they have resigned themselves to it and are, nevertheless, continuing to live.
I hope they are finding a means whereby they can survive-and not only survive, but expand. I do not know what provisions here can help them at all. They are not complaining about competition from periodicals published and printed abroad; the chief difficulty lay with publications printed in Canada but enjoying certain advantages because their editorial content and other facilities were supplied by the parent organization. This situation is to continue. As I say, there will be further discussion in this regard.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
I wish to thank the committee for having allowed me these few extra minutes. I will not abuse the generosity of hon. Members. As I indicated earlier, this budget resolution is composed of bits and pieces. There are items on which I have not commented, for example paragraph 13 which merely plugs loopholes. I should like to say something about item 15 which I think may discourage joint ventures by companies searching for oil and gas in the Western Provinces or even on the northern islands. I say this because it is no longer possible, as exploration goes further and further afield, for exploration to be carried out by an individual company. Even the largest one is now participating along with associates or competitors in their business in joint ventures to try to find a new field. Certainly under the regulations which apply in the Province of Alberta this is an eminently sound way of doing it, because if a new field is discovered and it is on only one Crown reserve, then the whole area may be parcelled out in leases and everbody gets a crack at it.
This certainly will contribute to the companies getting together, which is, again, a

sound point. But I am just wondering what the implications of paragraph 15 are going to be, because apparently the cost of acquiring the lease or licence cannot be passed back to the shareholder corporation, which frankly is the only one that is earning income; because the development syndicate or the development corporation that goes in to prove this particular well is not an income earner. I therefore rather suspect that what is going to happen is that the cost of acquiring leases which have been granted in previous years is going to be taken away this year under another form. We will discuss this further, Mr. Chairman, when the bill comes forward.

Mr. Chairman, having only five minutes at my disposal I shall just have to start to insert my knife in the ribs of the Minister of Finance and complete the evisceration at a later date. I may say that I was rather surprised that the Minister displayed such, shall I say disingenuousness, to give it no harder name, by repeating tonight the figures that he, I understand, provided his innocent and unfortunate Parliamentary Secretary who I am sorry to see is not in the House tonight, I am perfectly well aware that this is an honest misapprehension on his part. I suspect he had been misled by the Minister of Finance, who had not I am afraid at that time-in fact I am quite sure-read the amendment which was presented to the House on behalf of this party. In fact, Mr. Chairman, I recall meeting the Minister of Finance in the elevator and he was still hurling these ridiculous sums at me, and I pointed out that in fact there was another flaw in my amendment as it was written, and that anybody who earned $1,501, as he pointed out tonight, would have to pay on the $500 above $1,000.
However, tonight the Minister again produced these fantastic and astronomical figures which he provided for his unfortunate Parliamentary Secretary, and I am rather surprised that the Minister would stoop, again, to this disingenuousness instead of dealing with what was-and I admit it quite frankly -a shortcoming in my amendment; but a shortcoming made necessary by the fact that one cannot spell out all the consequences of action proposed in an amendment. What the Minister is telling us now is really this, that he is too incompetent to devise the graduation changes in the incomes just above the level of those whom I am proposing to remove altogether from the income tax
June 14, 1965

brackets. Many of us have suspected this, but what I find quite disturbing is the implication that not only is the Minister incompetent but that his officials, his advisers, his experts are also incompetent and are not able to make those minor adjustments in the income tax rates that would naturally, I would have thought-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I wonder if my hon. friend would permit a question?
Yes, do. I am always hoping you will dig yourself in deeper. Let us have it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is the hon. Member attempting now to say that he was not irresponsible and he was not even sloppy? Nobody can, surely, excuse him from one or other or both those charges.

Mr. Chairman, I am suggesting to the Minister that in an amendment-and perhaps if he had a little more experience in this House he would know this-presented in the middle of a debate in this House one does not spell out everything in detail.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I wonder if my hon. friend-
Perhaps the Minister can wait until I get through.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: He can contain himself.

Yes, he can contain himself. He asked me to contain myself. I contained myself until this moment, and look what happens. I found the Minister disingenuously repeating figures which were based, as he knew quite well this evening even though he was unaware of it the first time he persuaded his Parliamentary Secretary to produce them, on a gross misreading of the implications of my amendment.
You grossly misrepresented it to the public.

I suggest that it should have been obvious to anyone that the proposal which I made, which was to remove certain people altogether from the Minister's tax rolls, would necessitate some minor adjustments in the graduated income tax above that level to avoid the particular disabilities that the Minister pointed out tonight. Here is what he is telling us, that we are stuck forever 22620-1531

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion with this formula; that if we want to raise the income tax exemptions in this country, if we want to remove some other sections of the community from the Minister's tax rolls, we have to grant that exemption all the way up the scale. This is what he is telling us, in effect, this evening; that because you are going to eliminate certain people from the income tax rolls, therefore the result will be even more consideration for those in the higher income brackets.
I suggest to you, Sir, that this is either a revelation of incompetence on the part of the Minister or it is a revelation of the fact that he is not concerned with such matters as equity in the distribution of our income and the distribution of the burden of taxation for public services in this country.
May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Chairman, and complete my evisceration of the Minister at a later date.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, tomorrow we will continue with the discussion of the budget resolutions.
