maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY-REQUESTED REMOVAL OF UNSATISFACTORY PORTION
TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY-REQUESTED REMOVAL OF UNSATISFACTORY PORTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise at this time to complain, in the brief time allotted to me, of the condition of Highway No. 17 immediately west of the City of Ottawa, which is designated as part of the Trans-Canada Highway and which I respectfully submit is a very long way from coming up to the standards which are generally accepted as satisfactory with regard to the Trans-Canada Highway. I may say that it causes me some considerable embarrassment, as a Member from that part of the country, to be reprimanded by my fellow Members from such generally reputed poor provinces as Nova Scotia and Newfoundland, when they complain to me that this highway is far from the calibre of the Trans-Canada highway that they enjoy in their provinces.
This matter has been drawn to my attention by resolutions from the elected representatives of many of the municipalities in the
June 14, 1965

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion constituency I have the honour to represent, namely the Town of Amprior, the City of Renfrew, the Township of McNab, and the Township of Admaston. Also the Eastern Ontario Development Association has drawn this deplorable situation to my attention, and this prompted me to raise the matter in the House during the question period the other day, and to complain further here at this time.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
I quite appreciate that highways generally are within the provincial field of responsibility, but I do suggest that when a highway is part of the Trans-Canada Highway, this Government, this House, and in particular the Department of Public Works cannot suggest that they do not have some responsibility for its condition.
There is one very heartening thought about the sad condition of the highway, or tortuous trail, which I think has been properly referred to as a goat trail. As a boy, among my herolike movies was King of the Khyber Pass and, subsequently, The Lives of the Bengal Lancers, both motion pictures which were very popular in my day among young people. I understand that certain Hollywood people intend to make another movie of the Lives of the Bengal Lancers and, inasmuch as the roads in the Khyber Pass have been considerably improved since the 1930's, they feel that this stretch of No. 17 highway would be most adequate for the filming of the new version of the Lives of the Bengal Lancers. Therefore, there must be some modicum of benefit to the people in this regard. However, I think we would sooner have this part of the road brought up to the standard we expect for our Trans-Canada Highway.
Mind you, it is nothing new for the Ottawa Valley and, in particular, Eastern Ontario in general, to get the short end of the stick. As a matter of fact, when one talks about the short end of the stick, I suggest that in that part of the country we have not yet got the butt end of a good toothpick as our share in respect of matters such as roads, to which both the federal and provincial authorities contribute. In other areas we are used to being despoiled, just as Georgia was when Sherman marched through it. We have been despoiled of our rights to water resources as a result of the transmission of power to other locations instead of having industry come to the power source, as is the case in more enlightened provinces. We have, of course, the most expensive energy-electrical,
[Mr. Greened
petroleum and natural gas-of any part of the Province of Ontario, so we are used, as
I say, to being shortchanged in many ways. We do expect, however, to be able to get out of this part of the country with our produce, and to have some easy access to markets in order that we may share somewhat in the general bountiful advantages of this great province.
We are aware of the great metropolitan City of Toronto which received $50 million in regard to the Gardiner expressway, and $50 million in respect of the subway. In Toronto these days they have reached the point where on top of their roads, they have superhighways, and on top of the superhighways they have super, superhighways, and beneath it all they have a subway. The people I represent do not mind contributing to this great development in the metropolitan City of Toronto, as it is a wonderful area and we are very proud of its progress. Judging by the representation it sends to this House the people of Toronto are very wise politically. However, we would like to share somewhat in the bounties of this great province and we feel we can better do so if this section of the trans-Canada Highway is brought up to standard, so that we might have access to the great metropolitan markets.
I do suggest that the Federal Government has considerable responsibility in this regard. I understand that in the first instance highway No. 17 was designated as a main artery of the Trans-Canada Highway, but subsequently for some mysterious reason the main artery was diverted through Lindsay. There was a very eminent gentleman in the Provincial Government at that time who came from the Municipality of Lindsay, hence the main branch of the Trans-Canada Highway went through Lindsay, and our section of the highway for political reasons was designated as a second branch of the Trans-Canada Highway. That designation carried with it little green signs with little green maple leaves; but apart from that, no construction was to be observed.
So I suggest that the maple leaf is now the proud symbol of this nation and that it should only designate highways which are in fact of Trans-Canada standards. In the short time allotted to me I have but this to say: May we bring this highway up to Trans-Canada standards. As a Federal Government may we insist that if it is to be a Trans-Canada Highway it be brought up to Trans-Canada standards. Otherwise the vigilantes of the Ottawa valley will have little choice but
June 14, 1965
to tear down those little green maple leaves, because we know it is not in fact a trans-Canada Highway.

speakeroldname: Mr. G. Roy McWilliam (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY-REQUESTED REMOVAL OF UNSATISFACTORY PORTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the remarks of the hon. Member for Renfrew South (Mr. Greene) were listened to with a great deal of interest and I am sure they will be noted. However, I am informed by the officials of the Department of Public Works that this matter does not come within the jurisdiction of that Department or of any other Department of the Federal Government.
The section of highway 17 to which the hon. Member refers is not part of the official Trans-Canada Highway for which the Federal Government shared any costs. The maple leaf signs on this section of highway No. 17 were placed there by the Provincial Department of Highways with the Province bearing the cost. The object of these signs, I am told, is to indicate a provincial northern route connecting with the official Trans-Canada Highway. The Department takes the position that repairs and improvements to this section of highway 17 are entirely a provincial matter as the Federal Government did not share in the cost of the highway.

maintopic: FORESTRY-REMOVAL OF DEPARTMENTAL LABORATORIES TO SAULT STE. MARIE
FORESTRY-REMOVAL OF DEPARTMENTAL LABORATORIES TO SAULT STE. MARIE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret I have not got the capacity for understatement of the hon. Member for Renfrew South (Mr. Greene) to assist me in raising a matter about which I am rather irked. I see that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture is here to answer, I suppose, for the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve). It would have been too much for that great man to give us his presence this late in the evening. He is probably away in Quebec making the world safe for the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau).
The problem I want to touch on was raised in a question when I asked the Minister of Forestry if, when his estimates went before the appropriate committee of the House later this session, he would support a thorough investigation, including the calling of outside witnesses, with regard to the decision to put the regional forest research headquarters at
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion Sault Ste. Marie rather than retain them at Richmond Hill or Maple where they are now. This particular issue may seem rather small, but I think this action is the most outrageous blow struck at forestry science and forestry research in a long time. It is indefensible; it is stupid.
The Minister's answer was no, he would not support the calling of outside witnesses. I am going to be on the committee and I am going to try to see they are called. In any event, as a member of that committee I hope to interrogate the Minister and his officials so as to reveal that this great hero of cleanup in politics has been as guilty of pork barrel politics and patronage as any minister I have ever heard of. I have a letter here from a Mrs. K. C. von Althen of Richmond Hill who is close to the foresters there. She says in part:
While it may be too late to change the Minister's original decision, I sincerely believe that, for the benefit of the Department of Forestry, it should be pointed out in the House of Parliament that such a move is contrary to the best interests of future forest research in Ontario. In other words, if the old pork barrel approach is to be used, please say so and let the blame for future shortcoming be placed with the Minister rather than the practising scientists of the Department of Forestry.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
Who was it that the Minister of Forestry could not say no to? Was it the Prime Minister, whose constituency is close to Sault Ste. Marie? Was it the hon. Member for Algoma West (Mr. Nixon), who has been here so long and so quietly? Was it the Attorney General of Ontario, Mr. Wishart, who is the Member for Sault Ste. Marie and seems to have convinced the Provincial Department of Lands and Forests it should take a completely negative attitude on this question and not say yea or nay to this move?
I wanted to turn to the Minister's original announcement on February 18, and I quote from the press release:
"To establish our regional headquarters near the centre of major forest activity is, I feel, a sound decision," Mr. Sauve said. "All the various factors were carefully weighed and we consulted with all those involved."
There are lies in that statement. Consultation was inadequate. Sault Ste. Marie is not the centre of forest activity in Ontario. It is quite apparent that the factors that were looked at were partisan politics and superior pressure, if you want to put it that way.

You cannot blame me, therefore, for suggesting that there are some misstatements in the Minister's approach.
Later on, in a speech on March 23 to the Canadian Forestry Association, the Minister said:
In deciding on appropriate locations for our regional headquarters, we are guided by several important considerations, namely, the seat of Provincial forest authority-
That is in Toronto, not in Sault Ste. Marie, and Sault Ste. Marie is not even a regional headquarters.

There is not even a technical college established at Sault Ste. Marie.

Well, I cannot think of a more isolated part of Ontario, in a transportation sense, and one that has a smaller variety of corporations concerned with forest activities than the immediate Sault Ste. Marie area. Therefore, according to the Minister's own standards, the decision is wrong.
Later on, in this same speech, the Minister says:
In Ontario, we were faced with a particularly difficult situation, and we reached the decision that our regional headquarters should be in Sault Ste. Marie, which has the advantage of being geographically near the centre of the province and close to the forest industry.
He is getting a little bit closer to the truth. Sault Ste. Marie is close to the geographical centre of the Province and it is close, in terms of hundreds of miles, to the forest industry. The main point is that most of the research, research scientists, laboratories, library facilities, forestry associations, corporation headquarters, provincial headquarters and all their staffs are in the Toronto region, particularly at Richmond Hill and Maple.

I do not want to say anything more, other than that this move is going to lead to the resignations and loss to Canada and to the Government service, of some of the best people v/e have managed to get in the forestry service. subtopic: COMMUNIQUE FOLLOWING VISIT BY PRIME MINISTER OF INDIA

speechtext:
ministIre des affaires extSrieures
For Release Monday, June 14, 1965, at 08.00 hours E.D.S.T.

The Prime Minister of India, Mr. Lai Bahadur Shastri, paid an official visit to Canada June 10-14 at the invitation of the Canadian Government. During his stay in Canada the Prime Minister visited Ottawa and Niagara Falls and will spend June 14 in Montreal.
While in Ottawa, the Prime Minister of India visited the House of Commons and officially opened the Commonwealth Room in the Parliament Building. He laid a wreath at the War Memorial.
In Montreal, the Prime Minister of India will address a special convocation at McGill University at which an honorary degree will be conferred upon him. He will also call on the Mayor of Montreal at the City Hall.
The Prime Minister of India had discussions with Prime Minister Pearson, and the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Hon. Paul Martin; with the Minister of Finance, the Hon. Walter Gordon; with the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Hon. Mitchell Sharp; and with the Minister of Industry and Defence Production, the Hon. Charles M. Drury. The High Commissioner for Canada to India, the Hon. Roland Michener, and Canadian officials attended the discussions. The Prime Minister of India was assisted by the Indian High Commissioner to Canada, Mr. B. K. Acharya, Mr. L. K. Jha, Secretary to the Prime Minister, and Mr. R. Prasad, Joint Secretary to the Prime Minister.
In the course of their talks, the two Prime Ministers dealt with the wide range of relationships between India and Canada, with questions expected to arise at the forthcoming meeting of Commonwealth Heads of Government, and with the main international problems of the day. The talks disclosed understanding and respect for each other's point of view and a wide area of agreement on many world issues.
The two Prime Ministers expressed satisfaction with the friendship and cooperation which have at all times marked relations between India and Canada. They looked forward with confidence to the continuation of this warm relationship in the future.
Cooperation between the two countries extends to many fields, particularly the economic field. The Prime Minister of India expressed appreciation for the assistance extended by Canada to India under the Colombo Plan and for the cooperation between the two countries in promoting the economic development of India. The Prime Minister of Canada reiterated Canada's deep and continuing interest in the economic development of India and in the success of India's Five-year Plans.
Both Prime Ministers agreed on the urgent need to raise the standards of living of the peoples of developing countries. They recognized the responsibility of both the developed and developing countries to cooperate in this task and welcomed the establishment of the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development as an organization which could make a vital contribution toward the elimination of disparities in economic conditions through more rapid economic growth.
The two Prime Ministers re-affirmed their support for the United Nations and their desire to see the world organization develop into an effective instrument for the maintenance of international peace and security and for the promotion of understanding and co-operation among nations. The Prime Min-
June 14, 1965

isters noted that the present year marked the 20th anniversary of the United Nations and was being celebrated as International Cooperation Year. They hoped that it would usher in an era of increased United Nations activity and better international co-operation in the cause of world peace and prosperity.
They noted with concern and regret the difficulties that stood in the way of the functioning of the 19th Session of the General Assembly. They expressed their sincere hope that these difficulties would be overcome as a result of the discussions now going on in the Special Committee on Peacekeeping Operations and that the world body would emerge the stronger after the crisis.
It was also noted that both governments shared the desire to strengthen practical arrangements for United Nations peacekeeping. Both have been major participants in United Nations peacekeeping operations and continue to provide contingents of their armed forces for service in the United Nations Emergency Force in Gaza as they had done throughout the United Nations peacekeeping operations in the Congo. An Indian delegation participated in the discussions between military experts on the technical military aspects of United Nations peacekeeping which took place in Ottawa last November. The Prime Ministers agreed that, whatever the constitutional and other difficulties which stood in the way of collective responsibility for United Nations peacekeeping, it was imperative that a solution be found which would enable the United Nations to continue to fulfil this essential role in future.
The two Prime Ministers re-affirmed their support for the attainment of general and complete disarmament under effective international control. They discussed the great danger of proliferation of nuclear weapons and agreed that the 18-Nation Disarmament Committee should devote itself, as a matter of priority, to finding a solution to this problem. They called upon all states to abide by the spirit and provisions of the Treaty Banning Nuclear Weapons Tests in the Atmosphere, in Outer Space and Under Water. They emphasized the importance of taking early steps for the conclusion of a comprehensive Test Ban Treaty so as to cover underground tests as well.
The Prime Ministers expressed their deep regret and concern over the series of nuclear tests to which the People's Republic of China has devoted itself in defiance of a world opinion which strongly opposes the continuance of tests in any environment. These tests represent a setback to current efforts to achieve non-proliferation of nuclear weapons. The Prime Minister of Canada expressed particular satisfaction at India's decision not to use nuclear energy for other than peaceful purposes, despite India's technical capability to produce nuclear weapons.
They further expressed their satisfaction at their mutual association in the International Control Commissions in Indochina during the last eleven years. They recognized the difficulties in the functioning of the Commissions in the present circumstances.
While recognizing that it had not always been possible for Canadian and Indian views to coincide on every aspect of the consideration of the difficult problems arising before the Commissions, both Prime Ministers agreed that their mutual association in the Commissions had been useful, and re-affirmed their desire that their representatives in the Commissions should make every effort with a view to encouraging implementation of the Agreements, which it is the task of the Commission to supervise.
The Prime Ministers examined the situation in Vietnam and considered the measures open to them to try to bring peace to that country. They reviewed their efforts to try to interest the powers directly involved in a cease fire, in unconditional negotiations, and in greater international participation in and responsibility for bringing about and guaranteeing a cease fire and any agreement which might accompany or succeed it. They expressed their regret that lack of respect for the Cease Fire Agreement, as reported by the Commission in 1962, had led to the present higher level of hostilities. They were convinced that a purely military solution was neither practicable nor desirable.
They hoped that it might still be possible for the combatants to curtail hostilities or to initiate periods of cease fire which might become permanent; they also expressed the hope that their earlier proposals for negotiations without preconditions would still yield results. They agreed to work for a solution to the Vietnam problem which will enable the people of Vietnam to enjoy freedom and independence. Any settlement should be suitably guaranteed by the international community.
Both Prime Ministers expressed concern at the increasing tendency to use force for the settlement of disputes, and the Prime Min-

June 14, 1965
ister of Canada reiterated Canada's sympathy and support for India in her border conflict with China. He expressed the hope that the problem will be resolved peacefully and that China would agree to talks with India on the basis of the proposals of the six non-aligned countries formulated in Colombo in December 1962 which India had accepted.
The Prime Minister of India expressed his pleasure at visiting Canada and establishing contacts with Canadian leaders and people. He expressed deep appreciation of the warm hospitality extended to him and members of his party. He extended an invitation to the Prime Minister of Canada to visit India. The invitation was accepted with pleasure.
June 14, 1965
